tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

1	# **Senior Full-Stack Developer — Take-Home Technical Assessment**
2	
3	- Position Level: IC4/IC5
4	
5	- Time Allocation: 4-5 hours recommended
6	
7	- Submission Requirements: All deliverables + complete AI transcript
8	
9	## **Assessment Overview**
10	
11	This assessment evaluates your ability to design, build, and communicate full-stack solutions while leveraging AI tools as a force multiplier. You are assessed on four core performance axes:
12	
13	- Impact: Measurable outcomes and business value
14	
15	- Engineering Excellence: Technical depth, code quality, and best practices
16	
17	- People/Leadership: Communication, documentation clarity, and influence
18	
19	- Direction/Strategy: Long-term thinking, architectural vision, and scalability
20	
21	Critical Requirement: You must submit the complete transcript of your AI interactions (ChatGPT, Claude, or similar). Your use of AI is evaluated as a professional skill and not penalized. Show us how you prompt, iterate, and validate AI-generated outputs.
22	
23	## **Part 1: Recursive AI Logic & System Design**
24	
25	### **Scenario**
26	
27	You are building a multi-tenant project management platform where organizations can manage projects, tasks, team members, and track progress. Think of it as a simplified Linear or Jira.
28	
29	### **Task 1.1: Data Model Design**
30	
31	Using an AI tool, design a GraphQL schema + PostgreSQL data model that supports:
32	
33	- Multiple organizations, each with their own projects and team members
34	
35	- Projects containing tasks with assignees, priorities, statuses, labels, and due dates
36	
37	- Task comments and activity history (who changed what, when)
38	
39	- Role-based access control (owner, admin, member, viewer per organization)
40	
41	- Workspace-level settings and customizable task statuses per project
42	
43	Deliverable: GraphQL type definitions + SQL CREATE TABLE statements (or ORM model definitions)
44	
45	### **Task 1.2: Technical Documentation**
46	
47	Using the AI-generated schema from Task 1.1 as input, prompt your AI tool to generate comprehensive technical documentation covering:
48	
49	- Data model rationale and entity relationships
50	
51	- Query patterns for common operations (e.g., "get all overdue tasks assigned to me across projects")
52	
53	- Indexing strategy and performance considerations
54	
55	- Multi-tenancy isolation approach
56	
57	- Migration strategy for evolving the schema
58	
59	Deliverable: Technical documentation (2-3 pages, markdown format)
60	
61	### **Task 1.3: AI-Driven Architecture Critique**
62	
63	Prompt your AI tool to perform a critical analysis of the schema you designed, specifically identifying:
64	
65	- N+1 query risks in the GraphQL resolvers
66	
67	- Data consistency challenges (e.g., denormalized counters, status transitions)
68	
69	- Scalability bottlenecks at 100x current data volume
70	
71	- Security concerns (tenant isolation, authorization gaps)
72	
73	- Missing indexes or denormalization opportunities
74	
75	Then provide YOUR assessment: Do you agree with the AI's critique? What did it miss? What would you prioritize fixing first and why?
76	
77	Deliverable:
78	
79	1. AI critique output
80	
81	2. Your written analysis (500-750 words)
82	
83	## **Part 2: Full-Stack Implementation**
84	
85	### **Problem Statement**
86	
87	Build a Task Board feature for the project management platform described in Part 1. A Node.js GraphQL API serves the frontend.
88	
89	### **Task 2.1: Backend — GraphQL API**
90	
91	Design and implement a GraphQL API that:
92	
93	- Queries tasks with filtering (status, assignee, priority, due date range)
94	
95	- Supports cursor-based pagination for large task lists
96	
97	- Includes a summary/aggregation query (task counts by status, overdue count, tasks per assignee)
98	
99	- Handles authorization (users can only see tasks in organizations they belong to)
100	
101	Deliverable:
102	
103	1. GraphQL schema (type definitions)
104	
105	2. Resolver implementation (Node.js, minimum 80 lines of meaningful logic)
106	
107	3. Brief explanation of your design decisions (200-300 words)
108	
109	### **Task 2.2: Frontend — Task Board UI**
110	
111	Build a React component that:
112	
113	- Consumes the GraphQL API from Task 2.1
114	
115	- Displays tasks in a Kanban-style board (columns by status) or a filterable table — your choice
116	
117	- Shows summary statistics (total tasks, overdue count, distribution by priority)
118	
119	- Implements at least one data visualization (chart/graph)
120	
121	- Handles loading, error, and empty states gracefully
122	
123	Deliverable:
124	
125	1. React component code (TypeScript, using hooks)
126	
127	2. Brief explanation of state management and component architecture decisions (200-300 words)
128	
129	## **Part 3: Technical Communication & Product Thinking**
130	
131	### **Scenario**
132	
133	Your project management platform has grown to 500+ organizations. Users are reporting that the task board becomes unusably slow for projects with 2,000+ tasks. The current implementation fetches all tasks for a project in a single GraphQL query, renders the full Kanban board client-side, and re-fetches everything on every filter change or status update. Page load times are 6-8 seconds for large projects, and drag-and-drop reordering triggers a full refetch.
134	
135	### **Task 3.1: Technical RFC**
136	
137	Write an internal RFC (Request for Comments) proposing a solution. It must include:
138	
139	- Problem statement with data/metrics framing
140	
141	- Proposed approach (at least 2 options evaluated with trade-offs)
142	
143	- Recommended solution with implementation plan
144	
145	- Performance targets (what "good" looks like)
146	
147	- Rollout strategy (how to ship without breaking existing users)
148	
149	Target Audience: Your engineering team + product manager
150	
151	Deliverable: RFC document (2-3 pages, markdown)
152	
153	## **Submission Requirements**
154	
155	### **Required Deliverables**
156	
157	1. Part 1:
158	   - Schema definitions (GraphQL + SQL/ORM)
159	
160	   - Technical documentation (2-3 pages)
161	
162	   - AI critique + your analysis (500-750 words)
163	
164	2. Part 2:
165	   - Node.js GraphQL API code (schema + resolvers)
166	
167	   - React component code (TypeScript)
168	
169	   - Brief explanations for each
170	
171	3. Part 3:
172	   - RFC document (2-3 pages)
173	
174	4. AI Transcript:
175	   - Complete, unedited transcript of all AI interactions during this assessment
176	
177	   - Include all prompts, iterations, and refinements
178	
179	   - Add brief commentary on your prompting strategy
180	
181	### **Submission Format**
182	
183	- Single GitHub repository (preferred) or ZIP file
184	
185	- Organized directory structure with clear README
186	
187	- All documentation in markdown format
188	
189	- Code properly formatted with comments
190	
191	- Include a <mark>package.json</mark> so we can run your code
192	
193	### **Time Management Guidance**
194	
195	- Part 1 (System Design + AI Critique): 90-120 minutes
196	
197	- Part 2 (Implementation): 90-120 minutes
198	
199	- Part 3 (RFC): 60-90 minutes
200	
201	- Documentation & cleanup: 30 minutes
202	
203	Total: 4-5 hours
204	
205	## **Questions?**
206	
207	If you have clarifying questions about the assessment, please email [kcmanikanta@compliancefoundry.ai]. We encourage you to make reasonable assumptions when specifications are ambiguous, and to document them in your submission.
208	
209	Deadline: 7 days from assignment
210	
211	_This assessment evaluates real-world engineering skills. We value practical expertise, clear thinking, and effective use of modern AI tools to amplify your capabilities._

I've read the whole document. Here's what I understand the task to be, then the questions I need you to settle.

## What the assignment asks for

This is one connected story, and it reads best if the parts build on each other:

```
1.1 Schema (GraphQL + Postgres) ──► 1.2 Tech doc (built from that schema)
        │                           1.3 AI critique ──► your own analysis (500–750 words)
        ▼
2.1 GraphQL API (uses that schema) ──► 2.2 React TS task board (uses that API)
        │
        ▼
3.1 RFC: the board is slow at 2,000+ tasks; how we fix it
```

| Deliverable | Size limit |
|---|---|
| GraphQL SDL + SQL DDL (or ORM models) | — |
| Tech doc: rationale, query patterns, indexes, tenancy, migrations | 2–3 pages |
| Raw AI critique + **your** analysis | 500–750 words |
| API schema + resolvers (≥80 lines of real logic) + rationale | 200–300 words |
| React TS board (hooks, chart, loading/error/empty states) + rationale | 200–300 words |
| RFC (metrics, ≥2 options, plan, targets, rollout) | 2–3 pages |
| Complete AI transcript + notes on your prompting strategy | — |
| README, `package.json`, runs locally | — |

**What's graded:** how you use AI is scored as a skill: how you prompt, iterate and check the output. So this conversation is a deliverable in its own right.

## Questions

Each one has my suggested default. You can reply with something like "defaults fine except 3 and 7".

**Scope and design**

1. **Workspace vs organization.** The doc uses both words. Are they the same tenant, or does an organization contain several workspaces?
   *Default:* the same thing (like Linear). I'll note the assumption in the docs.
2. **Should Part 2 run on the Part 1 schema?**
   *Default:* yes. The Part 1 SQL becomes the real migrations, and Part 2 builds the board-related subset. That means the reviewer needs Postgres, which is something to settle when we pick the stack.
3. **Do we revise the schema after the critique?**
   *Default:* keep v1 frozen, so the critique still matches what it reviewed. Part 2 then uses a v2 with the top fixes applied, plus a short changelog. That makes the iteration visible.
4. **How much auth?**
   *Default:* no real signup or login. Seeded users, a signed JWT (or a dev header) to identify the user, and a "view as user" switcher in the UI to show that one tenant can't see another's data.
5. **Mutations.** Task 2.1 only asks for queries.
   *Default:* add one `updateTaskStatus` mutation with an optimistic UI update, so drag-and-drop works. That leads naturally into Part 3. The other option is read-only, which saves time.
6. **Kanban or table.**
   *Default:* Kanban, with a filter bar and per-column cursor pagination ("load more"). It fits the Part 3 scenario and already avoids the problem the RFC describes.
7. **Tests.** They aren't required.

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# What: files Git must never track for this repo.
# Why:  keeps the submission small and reproducible (deps/builds are regenerated
#       by `npm install` / `npm run build`) and keeps secrets out of history.
# Who:  applies to every contributor and to the reviewer cloning the repo.

node_modules/

dist/
build/
coverage/
*.tsbuildinfo

# Local environment + secrets. Only the documented template is tracked.
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

# Local embedded-Postgres (PGlite) data directory, if we use it — it is
# disposable state recreated by the migrate + seed scripts.
.pglite/

# Logs.
*.log
npm-debug.log*

# OS / editor noise.
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
.idea/
.vscode/*
!.vscode/extensions.json

# Claude Code machine-local settings. The shared notes in .claude/memory/
# are intentionally tracked (team-owned runbooks).
.claude/settings.local.json

# What: line-ending policy for the repository.
# Why:  this repo is authored on Windows but reviewed anywhere; storing LF in
#       Git means diffs, shell scripts and snapshot tests behave identically on
#       macOS/Linux/Windows regardless of each machine's core.autocrlf setting.
# How:  Git auto-detects text files and normalizes them to LF on commit.
* text=auto eol=lf

# Windows batch scripts are the one exception — cmd.exe expects CRLF.
*.cmd text eol=crlf
*.bat text eol=crlf

## Proposed tech stack

**Your machine:** Node 24.12 and npm 10.9. Docker is installed but its engine isn't running. pnpm, `psql` and `gh` aren't installed.

**Done so far:** I ran `git init` on `main` and added `.gitignore` plus `.gitattributes`. The `.gitattributes` forces LF line endings, since you're on Windows and the reviewers may not be. Nothing is committed yet.

| Layer | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Repo | npm workspaces: `api/`, `web/`, `docs/` | The reviewer needs no extra tools; one `npm install` |
| Language | TypeScript (strict) everywhere | |
| Database | Postgres 17 via **PGlite** (Postgres embedded in Node) by default; Docker Compose or `DATABASE_URL` for a real server | Reviewer runs `npm install && npm run setup && npm run dev` with nothing else installed |
| Migrations | Hand-written `.sql` files | The 1.1 SQL deliverable *is* the migration, so partial indexes, CHECK constraints and row-level security policies are visible as plain Postgres |
| Query layer | Kysely | Type-safe; builds dynamic filters and cursor pagination cleanly; not a full ORM |
| GraphQL server | GraphQL Yoga 6, schema written as SDL first | |
| Codegen | GraphQL Code Generator | One schema file produces typed resolvers on the server and typed queries in the client |
| Batching | DataLoader, one per request | Prevents N+1 queries (also material for 1.3) |
| Auth | `jose` (JWT signed with a dev secret) | |
| Validation | zod 4 | Env vars and inputs (page-size caps, date ranges) |
| Frontend | Vite + React 19 | |
| Data client | Apollo Client 4 | Its cache handles optimistically moving a card between two paginated columns |
| UI state | Filters in URL params, local UI state in hooks, no Redux/Zustand | The 2.2 explanation follows from this |
| Styling, drag-and-drop, charts | Tailwind 4, dnd-kit (keyboard accessible), Recharts 3 | |
| Tests | Vitest + React Testing Library; API tests run real GraphQL operations against a fresh PGlite database | Real Postgres without Docker, so CI works too |
| Quality | ESLint + Prettier, `npm run check`, a small GitHub Actions CI | |

### The four real choices

1. **How to run the database:** PGlite by default (my pick) or Docker only.
   - PGlite means zero setup and fast tests. But it allows only one connection, so it doesn't reflect concurrency.
   - I also need to confirm that Postgres row-level security works in PGlite. I'll test that first. If it doesn't, the row-level security demo runs on Docker and the checks in application code stay the main guard.
2. **Query layer:** SQL files + Kysely (my pick) or Drizzle.
   - With Drizzle you write less code and the schema lives in TypeScript, but the SQL becomes generated output.
   - With Kysely I keep the database type definitions by hand, about 100 lines.
   - I ruled out Prisma: it's weak on row-level security, partial indexes and custom cursor ordering.
3. **GraphQL server:** Yoga (my pick) or Apollo Server 5. It's a close call.
   - Yoga is lighter, hides internal errors from clients by default, and has plugins for query depth and cost limits.
   - Reviewers will recognise Apollo Server more readily.
4. **Client data layer:** Apollo Client 4 (my pick) or TanStack Query + `graphql-request`.
   - TanStack Query is simpler and smaller.
   - With TanStack, moving a card between columns optimistically means hand-editing several query caches.

**Versions:** TypeScript 7 (the new native compiler) and `graphql` 17 are the latest releases, and other tools' dependency ranges may not support them yet. When I set up the project, I'll pin the newest versions everything accepts and note why.

### Three small items (defaults in bold)

- **The assignment document in the repo:** it's the company's text, so if the repo is public I'd **leave it out** and summarise the task in the README.
- **CLAUDE.md:** your `.claude/memory/INDEX.md` says those notes load through a CLAUDE.md, but there isn't one, so new sessions won't pick up the comments rule. **Add a short CLAUDE.md** with commands, conventions and a pointer to the rule. It also shows reviewers how you set up your AI tooling, which helps the prompting-strategy write-up.
- **Comments rule:** I'll follow it with comments at file, function and block level that explain why and how, plus comments on any line that isn't obvious. I won't narrate trivial lines, since reviewers tend to read that as noise. Tell me if you want it stricter.

**Order after you confirm:**
1. Minimal setup: workspaces, PGlite, the migration runner, and the row-level security test. Then commit.
2. Part 1.1: design the schema, then run the DDL against real Postgres. Running it proves the AI-written SQL actually works, which is evidence for the transcript.

<pasted_content id="dc8f">
Why I still pick Kysely here

1. The graded deliverable is SQL. Task 1.1 asks for CREATE TABLE statements, and 1.2 and 1.3 analyze Postgres-specific things: partial indexes, CHECK constraints, row-level security. With Kysely, the reviewer reads hand-written, commented SQL, which fits your rule that all code carries detailed comments. With Drizzle, the SQL they read is generated and has no comments, and the commented version lives in a TypeScript file.
2. Our hardest queries are exactly where Kysely is stronger: row-tuple cursor comparison and FILTER aggregates.
3. The schema v1 → v2 plan for 1.3 is cleanest in SQL. The fixes after the critique become one new migration file, and that file is the changelog.

When I'd pick Drizzle instead

If you'd rather define the schema in TypeScript and have migrations generated, Drizzle is a good choice and I'd switch without arguing. You'd get correct types by default and a model-style schema their team will recognise. The cost is that the 1.1 deliverable becomes generated SQL, and we'd stay on stable 0.45 rather than the 1.0 beta.

I've written the tech stack doc: [docs/tech-stack-choice.md](docs/tech-stack-choice.md). It covers every tool with a one-line "what it is", why we picked it, what we turned down, and a short commented code sample using orgs, projects and tasks.

**The sections you asked for:**
- **PGlite vs Docker:** a one-line definition of PGlite, then a paragraph on WebAssembly and how Postgres's C code is compiled to it. There's a side-by-side comparison, plus the trade-offs we accept and how we handle each:
  - It allows only one connection, so its timings must not be quoted in the Part 3 RFC.
  - Its default user is a superuser and skips row-level security, so each request switches to a normal role first.
- **Kysely vs Drizzle:** your three points, now backed by the earlier spike. In that spike, Kysely had built-in support for the cursor comparison and the `FILTER` counts, while Drizzle needed raw `sql` for both. It also has the "when we'd pick Drizzle" paragraph and the date-parsing bug with its one-time fix.
- **Yoga vs PostGraphile:** four reasons it doesn't fit this task:
  - The spec grades hand-written resolvers.
  - We want the API shaped around the product, not the tables.
  - We want authorisation checked in the API, with row-level security as a second layer.
  - PostGraphile would hide the N+1 problem that 1.3 asks us to discuss.

  It also credits your PostGraphile background: we're borrowing its pattern of handing the logged-in user to Postgres for row-level security. Hasura and Apollo Server 5 are covered briefly.

**Things I added or decided that you should check:**
1. **A "why not Sequelize" section.** My notes say Compliance Foundry uses Sequelize, so their reviewers will likely ask. It says plainly that the spike showed Sequelize works on PGlite, explains why we still chose Kysely, and notes that keeping data access behind small repository modules makes swapping easy.
2. **How the app connects to PGlite.** It goes through `pglite-socket` with the standard `pg` driver, not a PGlite-specific Kysely plugin. That's the path the spike proved, and switching to a real Postgres is then just a `DATABASE_URL` change.
3. **Corrections to my earlier table** (the one in `image.png`): PGlite ships **Postgres 18**, not 17. Also, Apollo's optimistic update doesn't move a card between columns by itself; that needs a small cache `update` function, and the doc says so.
4. **What's verified and what isn't.** The PGlite and Kysely samples come from the spike and have been run. The `kysely-codegen` type generation and the other samples haven't; I'll confirm them during setup and update the doc if anything differs.

**Still open (my defaults in brackets):**
- The assignment document in the repo [leave it out].
- `image.png` in the repo root [leave it untracked; delete it if it was only a reference].
- A short CLAUDE.md [add one].

**Next step:** project setup. That means npm workspaces, TypeScript/ESLint/Prettier, PGlite with the socket and type fixes, the migration runner, and a row-level security check. Then one commit with this doc included. Shall I start?

# Migrations

These hand-written SQL files are the **single source of truth** for the database schema. TypeScript types (`api/src/db/types.ts`) are generated from them by `npm run db:codegen -w api`.

## Rules

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| Name files `NNNN_snake_case_description.sql` (e.g. `0001_initial_schema.sql`) | Kysely applies migrations in name order; a fixed 4-digit prefix keeps `0010` after `0009`. Other names are rejected. |
| **Never edit a migration that has been committed**; add a new one | Environments that already applied it would silently diverge from the file. |
| Forward-only: there are no `down` migrations | Rolling back by hand-written `down` scripts is rarely tested and often destroys data. Fixes ship as new migrations. |
| Comment every table, column group, constraint and index with its *why* | The SQL is a reviewed deliverable, not generated output. |
| After adding a migration, run `npm run db:codegen -w api` and commit `src/db/types.ts` | Keeps the query types in lock-step with the schema (CI runs `--verify`). |

## How they run

`npm run db:migrate -w api` applies pending files through Kysely's `Migrator`. On Postgres, the whole pending batch runs in **one transaction**: if any file fails, none of them are applied. Applied migrations are recorded in the `kysely_migration` table.

You write queries that read like SQL (`selectFrom('tasks').where(...)`), and the compiler checks table and column names and infers the shape of each result row. It isn't an ORM: there are no model classes, no lazy loading and no hidden queries. One builder chain compiles to exactly one SQL statement.

9	| Name files `NNNN_snake_case_description.sql` (e.g. `0001_initial_schema.sql`)          | Kysely applies migrations in name order; a fixed 4-digit prefix keeps `0010` after `0009`. Other names are rejected. |
10	| **Never edit a migration that has been committed**; add a new one                      | Environments that already applied it would silently diverge from the file.                                           |
11	| Forward-only: there are no `down` migrations                                           | Rolling back by hand-written `down` scripts is rarely tested and often destroys data. Fixes ship as new migrations.  |
12	| Comment every table, column group, constraint and index with its _why_                 | The SQL is a reviewed deliverable, not generated output.                                                             |
13	| After adding a migration, run `npm run db:codegen -w api` and commit `src/db/types.ts` | Keeps the query types in lock-step with the schema (CI runs `--verify`).                                             |
14	
15	## How they run
16	
17	`npm run db:migrate -w api` applies pending files through Kysely's `Migrator`. On Postgres, the whole pending batch runs in **one transaction**: if any file fails, none of them are applied. Applied migrations are recorded in the `kysely_migration` table.

53	### Trade-offs we accept, and how we handle them
54	
55	- **One connection only.** The pool is capped at `max: 1`, so queries run one at a time. That's fine for a demo and for tests, but **PGlite timings must not be quoted as production performance** (relevant to the Part 3 RFC).
56	- **The default user is a superuser, and superusers bypass row-level security.** Each request transaction switches to a non-privileged role (`SET LOCAL ROLE app_user`) before querying, which also matches how production should run.
57	- **Newer, smaller ecosystem than the official Docker image.** If a PGlite issue blocks us, the `DATABASE_URL` path is the fallback.

60	// db/pglite.ts — WHERE: dev server + test setup. WHEN: process start / each test file.
61	// WHAT: boots an embedded Postgres and exposes it on a local TCP port, so the rest of
62	// the app talks to it exactly like a real Postgres server (via the standard `pg` driver).
63	import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite';
64	import { PGLiteSocketServer } from '@electric-sql/pglite-socket';
65	import pg from 'pg';
66	
67	const pglite = await PGlite.create('./.pglite'); // data persisted in ./.pglite (git-ignored)
68	const server = new PGLiteSocketServer({ db: pglite, port: 0 }); // port 0 = pick any free port
69	await server.start();
70	const port = (server.server.address() as { port: number }).port;
71	
72	// max: 1 — PGlite serves one connection at a time; a bigger pool would just queue.
73	export const pool = new pg.Pool({
74	  connectionString: `postgres://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:${port}/postgres`,
75	  max: 1,
76	});
77	```

81	## 4. Schema & query layer: hand-written SQL migrations + Kysely (not Drizzle)
82	
83	**What Kysely is:** a type-safe SQL query builder for TypeScript. You write queries that read like SQL (`selectFrom('tasks').where(...)`), and the compiler checks table and column names and infers the shape of each result row. It isn't an ORM: there are no model classes, no lazy loading and no hidden queries. One builder chain compiles to exactly one SQL statement.
84	
85	**How the pieces fit:**
86	
87	1. The schema lives in numbered, commented `.sql` migration files. They are the single source of truth.
88	2. Kysely's built-in `Migrator` applies them in order, keeping a tracking table and a lock.
89	3. TypeScript row types are generated from the migrated database (`kysely-codegen`), so the types can't drift from the SQL.
90	
91	### Why Kysely over Drizzle
92	
93	1. **The graded deliverable is SQL.** Task 1.1 asks for `CREATE TABLE` statements, and 1.2 and 1.3 analyse Postgres-specific features: partial indexes, CHECK constraints, row-level security. With Kysely, the reviewer reads hand-written, commented SQL, which also satisfies the project rule that all code carries detailed comments. With Drizzle, the SQL the reviewer reads is generated and has no comments; the commented version lives in a TypeScript file.
94	2. **Our hardest queries are where Kysely is strongest.** We ran the same two queries side by side in a spike:

366	  expect(res.errors?.[0]?.extensions?.code).toBe('FORBIDDEN');
367	});
368	```

- **Kysely uses `CamelCasePlugin`.** TypeScript is `camelCase`, SQL is `snake_case`. Identifiers inside raw `sql` template text must be `snake_case`.
- **pg type parsers (`api/src/db/pool.ts`)**: `DATE` comes back as a `'YYYY-MM-DD'` string, and `int8` as a number (it throws if the value isn't a safe integer). Don't change these without updating codegen options and tests.

- **Row-level security on PGlite.** The default user is a superuser, which bypasses RLS, so request transactions must `SET LOCAL ROLE`. Read custom settings with `nullif(current_setting('app.x', true), '')`: after first use, a setting reads as `''`, not NULL.
- **Workflow.** Go phase by phase as agreed with the user, wait for a go-ahead before starting a new phase, and run `npm run check` before calling anything done.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run setup` | Apply migrations to the embedded dev database (`api/.pglite`) |
| `npm run check` | Typecheck, lint, format check, verify generated types, run tests (also run in CI) |

| `npm run db:codegen -w api` | Regenerate Kysely types from the migrations (`-- --verify` to check only) |

# Task Board: Multi-tenant Project Management (Take-Home)

A simplified Linear/Jira-style platform built for the Compliance Foundry Senior Full-Stack assessment. It has three parts:

- A PostgreSQL data model.
- A Node.js GraphQL API.
- A React + TypeScript task board.

The design documents, AI critique and RFC sit alongside the code.

> **Status:** project setup is complete. Parts 1–3 are in progress, and this README will map every deliverable once they're done.

## Quick start

Requires **Node.js ≥ 22.12** (developed on 24.12). No database install and no Docker: PostgreSQL runs embedded via [PGlite](docs/tech-stack-choice.md#3-database-runtime-postgresql-via-pglite-not-docker).

```bash
npm install
npm run setup   # create the embedded database and apply migrations
npm run check   # typecheck, lint, format, generated-types check, tests
```

To use a real PostgreSQL server instead, copy `api/.env.example` to `api/.env` and set `DATABASE_URL`.

## Repository layout

```
api/                 Node.js GraphQL API (TypeScript)
  db/migrations/     Hand-written SQL migrations, the schema's source of truth
  src/db/            Connection pool, embedded Postgres, migrator, generated types
  src/scripts/       CLI scripts: db:migrate, db:reset, db:codegen
  test/              Integration tests against real (embedded) Postgres
docs/                Design docs, critique, RFC, tech stack rationale
```

## Documents

- [Tech stack choice](docs/tech-stack-choice.md): what every tool is, why we chose it, and what we turned down.

## Assumptions

- "Organization" and "workspace" are the same tenant concept; the code and docs say "organization".
- Authentication is out of scope. Seeded users get signed development tokens, and authorization is fully enforced.

# What: continuous integration for every push to main and every pull request.
# Why:  the exact gate a developer runs locally (`npm run check`) also guards every
#       change: typecheck → lint → formatting → generated DB types are fresh → tests.
#       No Postgres service container is needed — tests boot embedded PGlite.
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

# A newer push to the same branch makes an in-flight run pointless — cancel it.
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Same Node major as local development (.nvmrc); npm cache keyed on the lockfile.
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm

      # `npm ci` installs exactly what package-lock.json records (no silent upgrades).
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run check

# CLAUDE.md

Working agreement for AI coding assistants on this repo. Humans: see README.md.

## Project

Take-home for Compliance Foundry: a multi-tenant project-management platform (organizations → projects → tasks). Deliverables are mapped in README.md, and stack rationale is in `docs/tech-stack-choice.md`.

## Rules

- **Comment all code.** Every new or modified block carries detailed comments covering what / why / how (plus which / where / when / who where relevant). Full rule: `.claude/memory/feedback_code_comments_mandatory.md`; team notes index: `.claude/memory/INDEX.md`.
- **Say "organization" everywhere.** Organization and workspace are the same tenant concept.
- **The SQL migrations in `api/db/migrations/` are the schema's source of truth.** They are forward-only. Never edit a committed migration; add a new one, then run `npm run db:codegen -w api` and commit the regenerated `api/src/db/types.ts`.
- **Kysely uses `CamelCasePlugin`.** TypeScript is `camelCase`, SQL is `snake_case`. Identifiers inside raw `sql` template text must be `snake_case`.
- **pg type parsers (`api/src/db/pool.ts`)**: `DATE` comes back as a `'YYYY-MM-DD'` string, and `int8` as a number (it throws if the value isn't a safe integer). Don't change these without updating codegen options and tests.
- **PGlite is one Postgres session.** Keep the pool and socket at one connection. Its timings are not production numbers.
- **Row-level security on PGlite.** The default user is a superuser, which bypasses RLS, so request transactions must `SET LOCAL ROLE`. Read custom settings with `nullif(current_setting('app.x', true), '')`: after first use, a setting reads as `''`, not NULL.
- **Workflow.** Go phase by phase as agreed with the user, wait for a go-ahead before starting a new phase, and run `npm run check` before calling anything done.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run setup` | Apply migrations to the embedded dev database (`api/.pglite`) |
| `npm run check` | Typecheck, lint, format check, verify generated types, run tests (also run in CI) |
| `npm test` | Tests only (each file boots a fresh in-memory PGlite) |
| `npm run db:migrate -w api` | Apply pending migrations |
| `npm run db:reset -w api` | Delete and rebuild the embedded dev database (refuses if `DATABASE_URL` is set) |
| `npm run db:codegen -w api` | Regenerate Kysely types from the migrations (`-- --verify` to check only) |

# Task Board: Multi-tenant Project Management (Take-Home)

A simplified Linear/Jira-style platform built for the Compliance Foundry Senior Full-Stack assessment. It has three parts:

- A PostgreSQL data model.
- A Node.js GraphQL API.
- A React + TypeScript task board.

The design documents, AI critique and RFC sit alongside the code.

> **Status:** project setup is complete. Parts 1–3 are in progress, and this README will map every deliverable once they're done.

## Quick start

Requires **Node.js ≥ 22.12** (developed on 24.12). No database install and no Docker: PostgreSQL runs embedded via [PGlite](docs/tech-stack-choice.md#3-database-runtime-postgresql-via-pglite-not-docker).

```bash
npm install
npm run setup   # create the embedded database and apply migrations
npm run check   # typecheck, lint, format, generated-types check, tests
```

To use a real PostgreSQL server instead, copy `api/.env.example` to `api/.env` and set `DATABASE_URL`.

## Repository layout

```
api/                 Node.js GraphQL API (TypeScript)
  db/migrations/     Hand-written SQL migrations, the schema's source of truth
  src/db/            Connection pool, embedded Postgres, migrator, generated types
  src/scripts/       CLI scripts: db:migrate, db:reset, db:codegen
  test/              Integration tests against real (embedded) Postgres
docs/                Design docs, critique, RFC, tech stack rationale
```

## Documents

- [Tech stack choice](docs/tech-stack-choice.md): what every tool is, why we chose it, and what we turned down.

## Assumptions

- "Organization" and "workspace" are the same tenant concept; the code and docs say "organization".
- Authentication is out of scope. Seeded users get signed development tokens, and authorization is fully enforced.

Project setup is finished and committed as `9f463c2`. `npm run check` passes: typecheck, lint, formatting, the generated-types check and 11 database tests. I also ran each database script for real, including both safety refusals in `db:reset`.

## What was built

| Area | Files |
|---|---|
| Repo tooling | `package.json` (npm workspaces), TypeScript strict, ESLint, Prettier, `.editorconfig`, `.nvmrc`, CI workflow |
| Database layer | `api/src/db/`: embedded PGlite, connection pool, migration runner, generated types |
| Scripts | `db:migrate`, `db:reset` (refuses on a real server or a folder outside `api/`), `db:codegen` (plus `--verify`) |
| Tests | `api/test/db.test.ts` |
| Docs | `CLAUDE.md`, README stub, migrations README, updated `docs/tech-stack-choice.md` |

**How a query reaches the database:**
1. Config is read and validated from env.
2. If `DATABASE_URL` isn't set, PGlite starts inside Node and listens on a local port.
3. The standard `pg` driver connects to that port, with our fixes for dates and counts.
4. Kysely builds typed queries on top.

With `DATABASE_URL` set, steps 3–4 are unchanged and only step 2 is skipped.

## Things setup turned up

1. **TypeScript 7 isn't usable yet.** The lint tooling only supports versions below 6.1, so I pinned 6.0.3.
2. **Kysely 0.29 moved its migrator** to `kysely/migration`. The typecheck caught it; my knowledge of the API was out of date.
3. **The real reason PGlite needs one connection is stronger than I first stated.** PGlite is a single Postgres session, so two connections would share it, and one request's open transaction or `SET LOCAL ROLE` could leak into another request. Both the socket server and the pool are capped at 1.
4. **Part 1's row-level security policies need `nullif`.** I confirmed with a throwaway script that once a request has set `app.organization_id`, it reads as `''` rather than NULL, and `''::int` throws. A naive policy would therefore error on later requests instead of returning no rows. The tests pin the safe version.
5. **Each batch of migrations runs in one transaction.** That rules out `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in migration files; 1.2's migration strategy will cover it.
6. **A Part 2 issue to design for:** JavaScript dates lose Postgres's microsecond precision, so a pagination cursor built on `created_at` can skip or repeat tasks. Postgres 18's built-in `uuidv7()` (time-ordered ids) is a clean fix.

## Decisions I applied

- **Naming:** Kysely's `CamelCasePlugin`, so SQL stays `snake_case` and TypeScript is `camelCase`.
- **Your open items, with my defaults:** the assignment brief is git-ignored, and CLAUDE.md is added and points to your comments rule.
- **CI:** it uses the current `actions/*@v7` (I looked them up). It hasn't run yet, because there's no GitHub remote; it will run on your first push.

- The GraphQL SDL.
- `0001_initial_schema.sql`, actually run against Postgres 18.
- Regenerated types.
- Tests proving the constraints and tenant isolation work.

- An ordering key for Kanban card order.

- The shape of the activity log.
- Soft deletes.
- Row-level security policies.

-- =============================================================================
-- 0001_foundation.sql — request role, `app` schema, shared trigger helpers
-- =============================================================================
-- Schema v1 (Task 1.1). Frozen once reviewed: fixes ship as new migrations.
--
-- What: the primitives every later migration builds on; no domain tables here.
-- Why:  keeping infrastructure out of the table migrations lets 0002–0004 read
--       as pure data modelling, and 0005 as pure access control.
--
-- Conventions used throughout the schema (explained once, here):
--   * Primary keys are `uuid DEFAULT uuidv7()` (built into Postgres 18). v7 UUIDs
--     start with a millisecond timestamp, so new rows land at the right-hand edge
--     of the B-tree (like a bigserial, no random page splits as with v4), yet they
--     are globally unique, safe to expose in URLs (no "you are customer #312"
--     leakage) and can be generated by clients for optimistic UI.
--   * Every tenant-owned row carries `organization_id`, even when it is derivable
--     through a parent. Composite foreign keys (organization_id, parent_id) then
--     make a cross-tenant reference impossible, and row-level security (0005) can
--     filter every table without joins.
--   * Timestamps are `timestamptz` (an instant); due dates are `date` (a calendar
--     day with no zone — "due on the 20th" must not shift with the viewer's zone).
--   * Lengths and formats are CHECK constraints, so every writer (API, scripts,
--     a future service) gets the same validation as the GraphQL layer.
-- =============================================================================


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Request role: app_user
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Every API request runs inside one transaction that begins with
--     SET LOCAL ROLE app_user;
--     SELECT set_config('app.user_id', '<authenticated user uuid>', true);
-- app_user owns no tables, so row-level security policies (0005) always apply to
-- it. The schema owner (the role running these migrations) bypasses RLS; it is
-- used only by migrations, seeds and the SECURITY DEFINER functions below.
-- In production the API would log in as a role that is a member of app_user.
--
-- Roles are cluster-wide objects (shared by every database on the server), so
-- this is "create if missing" instead of a plain CREATE ROLE.
DO $$
BEGIN
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_catalog.pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'app_user') THEN
    CREATE ROLE app_user NOLOGIN;
  END IF;
END
$$;


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- `app` schema: infrastructure functions (auth helpers, trigger functions)
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Keeps `public` = data only, which is also exactly what kysely-codegen turns
-- into TypeScript types.
CREATE SCHEMA app;

-- Functions are executable by PUBLIC by default. Lock the schema down; 0005
-- grants app_user exactly the functions it needs.
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA app REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC;


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- app.current_user_id() — who is making this request?
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Reads the transaction-local setting written at the start of each request.
-- `true` = return NULL instead of erroring when the setting was never set.
-- `nullif(…, '')`: once a custom setting has been used in a session, Postgres
-- reports it as '' (not NULL) after that transaction ends, and ''::uuid would
-- throw. Verified in api/test/db.test.ts — this keeps "no user" = NULL, which
-- every policy treats as "sees nothing" (fail closed).
-- Also used as a column DEFAULT (tasks.created_by, …) so authorship cannot be
-- spoofed: app_user is not granted INSERT on those columns (0005).
CREATE FUNCTION app.current_user_id() RETURNS uuid
LANGUAGE sql STABLE PARALLEL SAFE
AS $$
  SELECT nullif(pg_catalog.current_setting('app.user_id', true), '')::uuid
$$;


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- app.set_updated_at() — keeps `updated_at` honest
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- BEFORE UPDATE trigger body shared by every table with an `updated_at` column.
-- Doing it in the database means no code path can forget it. `now()` is the
-- transaction start time, so all rows changed in one request share a timestamp.
CREATE FUNCTION app.set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.updated_at := pg_catalog.now();
  RETURN NEW;
END
$$;

-- =============================================================================
-- 0002_tenancy.sql — users, organizations (tenants), settings, memberships/roles
-- =============================================================================
-- Schema v1 (Task 1.1).
--
-- Model: a USER is a global identity (one login, many organizations). An
-- ORGANIZATION is the tenant boundary — "organization" and "workspace" are the
-- same concept in this product. ORGANIZATION_MEMBERS is the many-to-many link that
-- also carries the user's ROLE in that organization (RBAC is per organization).
-- =============================================================================


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Roles, in ascending order of power.
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- A Postgres enum (not text + CHECK) because enum values compare by declaration
-- order: `role >= 'admin'` means "admin or owner", which is how every permission
-- check in 0005 is written. Adding a role later is `ALTER TYPE … ADD VALUE …
-- BEFORE/AFTER`, which preserves the ordering.
--   viewer — read-only access to everything in the organization
--   member — creates and edits tasks, comments, labels
--   admin  — manages projects, statuses, settings and non-owner members
--   owner  — everything, incl. managing owners and deleting the organization
CREATE TYPE organization_role AS ENUM ('viewer', 'member', 'admin', 'owner');


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- users — global identities
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Authentication is out of scope (no password/IdP columns); in production this row
-- would be keyed to an identity provider subject.
CREATE TABLE users (
  id            uuid        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),

-- =============================================================================
-- 0001_foundation.sql — request role, `app` schema, shared trigger helpers
-- =============================================================================
-- Schema v1 (Task 1.1). Frozen once reviewed: fixes ship as new migrations.
--
-- What: the primitives every later migration builds on; no domain tables here.
-- Why:  keeping infrastructure out of the table migrations lets 0002–0004 read
--       as pure data modelling, and 0005 as pure access control.
--
-- Conventions used throughout the schema (explained once, here):
--   * Primary keys are `uuid DEFAULT uuidv7()` (built into Postgres 18). v7 UUIDs
--     start with a millisecond timestamp, so new rows land at the right-hand edge
--     of the B-tree (like a bigserial, no random page splits as with v4), yet they
--     are globally unique, safe to expose in URLs (no "you are customer #312"
--     leakage) and can be generated by clients for optimistic UI.
--   * Every tenant-owned row carries `organization_id`, even when it is derivable
--     through a parent. Composite foreign keys (organization_id, parent_id) then
--     make a cross-tenant reference impossible, and row-level security (0005) can
--     filter every table without joins.
--   * Timestamps are `timestamptz` (an instant); due dates are `date` (a calendar
--     day with no zone — "due on the 20th" must not shift with the viewer's zone).
--   * Lengths and formats are CHECK constraints, so every writer (API, scripts,
--     a future service) gets the same validation as the GraphQL layer.
-- =============================================================================


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Request role: app_user
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Every API request runs inside one transaction that begins with
--     SET LOCAL ROLE app_user;
--     SELECT set_config('app.user_id', '<authenticated user uuid>', true);
-- app_user owns no tables, so row-level security policies (0005) always apply to
-- it. The schema owner (the role running these migrations) bypasses RLS; it is
-- used only by migrations, seeds and the SECURITY DEFINER functions below.
-- In production the API would log in as a role that is a member of app_user.
--
-- Roles are cluster-wide objects (shared by every database on the server), so
-- this is "create if missing" instead of a plain CREATE ROLE.
DO $$
BEGIN
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_catalog.pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'app_user') THEN
    CREATE ROLE app_user NOLOGIN;
  END IF;
END
$$;


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- `app` schema: infrastructure functions (auth helpers, trigger functions)
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Keeps `public` = data only, which is also exactly what kysely-codegen turns
-- into TypeScript types.
CREATE SCHEMA app;

-- Functions are executable by PUBLIC by default. Lock the schema down; 0005
-- grants app_user exactly the functions it needs.
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA app REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC;


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- app.current_user_id() — who is making this request?
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Reads the transaction-local setting written at the start of each request.
-- `true` = return NULL instead of erroring when the setting was never set.
-- `nullif(…, '')`: once a custom setting has been used in a session, Postgres
-- reports it as '' (not NULL) after that transaction ends, and ''::uuid would
-- throw. Verified in api/test/db.test.ts — this keeps "no user" = NULL, which
-- every policy treats as "sees nothing" (fail closed).
-- Also used as a column DEFAULT (tasks.created_by, …) so authorship cannot be
-- spoofed: app_user is not granted INSERT on those columns (0005).
CREATE FUNCTION app.current_user_id() RETURNS uuid
LANGUAGE sql STABLE PARALLEL SAFE
AS $$
  SELECT nullif(pg_catalog.current_setting('app.user_id', true), '')::uuid
$$;


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- app.set_updated_at() — keeps `updated_at` honest
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- BEFORE UPDATE trigger body shared by every table with an `updated_at` column.
-- Doing it in the database means no code path can forget it. `now()` is the
-- transaction start time, so all rows changed in one request share a timestamp.
CREATE FUNCTION app.set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.updated_at := pg_catalog.now();
  RETURN NEW;
END
$$;

  IF OLD.role = 'owner'
     AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.organizations o WHERE o.id = OLD.organization_id)
     AND NOT EXISTS (
       SELECT 1 FROM public.organization_members m
        WHERE m.organization_id = OLD.organization_id AND m.role = 'owner')
  THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'organization % must keep at least one owner', OLD.organization_id
      USING ERRCODE = 'check_violation',
            HINT = 'Promote another member to owner before removing or demoting this one.';
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;
END
$$;

CREATE CONSTRAINT TRIGGER organization_members_keep_an_owner
  AFTER UPDATE OF role OR DELETE ON organization_members
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.organization_keeps_an_owner();

-- =============================================================================
-- 0002_tenancy.sql — users, organizations (tenants), settings, memberships/roles
-- =============================================================================
-- Schema v1 (Task 1.1).
--
-- Model: a USER is a global identity (one login, many organizations). An
-- ORGANIZATION is the tenant boundary — "organization" and "workspace" are the
-- same concept in this product. ORGANIZATION_MEMBERS is the many-to-many link that
-- also carries the user's ROLE in that organization (RBAC is per organization).
-- =============================================================================


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Roles, in ascending order of power.
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- A Postgres enum (not text + CHECK) because enum values compare by declaration
-- order: `role >= 'admin'` means "admin or owner", which is how every permission
-- check in 0005 is written. Adding a role later is `ALTER TYPE … ADD VALUE …
-- BEFORE/AFTER`, which preserves the ordering.
--   viewer — read-only access to everything in the organization
--   member — creates and edits tasks, comments, labels
--   admin  — manages projects, statuses, settings and non-owner members
--   owner  — everything, incl. managing owners and deleting the organization
CREATE TYPE organization_role AS ENUM ('viewer', 'member', 'admin', 'owner');


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- users — global identities
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Authentication is out of scope (no password/IdP columns); in production this row
-- would be keyed to an identity provider subject.
CREATE TABLE users (
  id            uuid        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  email         text        NOT NULL,
  display_name  text        NOT NULL,
  avatar_url    text,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

  CONSTRAINT users_email_unique UNIQUE (email),
  -- Stored normalised (trimmed + lower-case), so the plain UNIQUE above is
  -- effectively case-insensitive without the citext extension.
  CONSTRAINT users_email_normalized CHECK (email = lower(btrim(email)) AND email LIKE '%_@_%'),
  CONSTRAINT users_display_name_length CHECK (char_length(btrim(display_name)) BETWEEN 1 AND 100),
  CONSTRAINT users_avatar_url_length CHECK (avatar_url IS NULL OR char_length(avatar_url) <= 2048)
);

CREATE TRIGGER users_set_updated_at
  BEFORE UPDATE ON users
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.set_updated_at();


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- organizations — the tenant
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE organizations (
  id          uuid        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  name        text        NOT NULL,
  -- URL identifier: app.example.com/acme/… Lower-case, digits, inner hyphens.
  slug        text        NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

  CONSTRAINT organizations_slug_unique UNIQUE (slug),
  CONSTRAINT organizations_slug_format CHECK (slug ~ '^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]{0,46}[a-z0-9])?$'),
  CONSTRAINT organizations_name_length CHECK (char_length(btrim(name)) BETWEEN 1 AND 100)
);

CREATE TRIGGER organizations_set_updated_at
  BEFORE UPDATE ON organizations
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.set_updated_at();


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- organization_settings — organization-level (workspace-level) settings
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- One row per organization, with TYPED columns rather than a jsonb bag: each
-- setting gets a real type, a default and a CHECK, and adding a setting is a
-- reviewed migration. (jsonb is the right call only for user-defined/unknown keys.)
-- Kept apart from `organizations` because settings are edited by a different
-- audience (admins) and change on a different cadence than the tenant identity.
CREATE TABLE organization_settings (
  organization_id              uuid        PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES organizations (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- IANA zone that defines "today" for the organization — and therefore what
  -- "overdue" means (a task due on the 20th is overdue from the 21st *there*).
  timezone                     text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'UTC',
  -- First day of the week in calendar views: 0 = Sunday … 6 = Saturday (ISO: 1).
  week_starts_on               smallint    NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  -- Lets admins decide whether plain members may create projects; enforced by
  -- the projects INSERT policy in 0005 (settings drive authorization).
  members_can_create_projects  boolean     NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  updated_at                   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

  -- Evaluating a zone conversion rejects unknown zone names ("Mars/Olympus") with
  -- an error, so only real IANA zones are ever stored.
  CONSTRAINT organization_settings_timezone_valid CHECK ((now() AT TIME ZONE timezone) IS NOT NULL),
  CONSTRAINT organization_settings_week_starts_on_range CHECK (week_starts_on BETWEEN 0 AND 6)
);

CREATE TRIGGER organization_settings_set_updated_at
  BEFORE UPDATE ON organization_settings
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.set_updated_at();

-- Every organization always has a settings row (created with the defaults), so
-- readers never need a LEFT JOIN + COALESCE. SECURITY DEFINER: the settings row
-- is created on behalf of whoever created the organization, whatever their grants.
CREATE FUNCTION app.organizations_create_settings() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = ''
AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO public.organization_settings (organization_id) VALUES (NEW.id);
  RETURN NULL; -- AFTER trigger: return value ignored
END
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER organizations_create_settings
  AFTER INSERT ON organizations
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.organizations_create_settings();


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- organization_members — who belongs to which organization, with which role
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE organization_members (
  organization_id  uuid              NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- Deleting a user removes their memberships (their tasks become unassigned via
  -- the ON DELETE SET NULL on tasks — see 0003).
  user_id          uuid              NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  role             organization_role NOT NULL DEFAULT 'member',
  created_at       timestamptz       NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), -- "joined at"
  updated_at       timestamptz       NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

  -- PK serves "who is in organization X" (organization_id first) and is the
  -- target of tasks' composite assignee FK.
  PRIMARY KEY (organization_id, user_id)
);

-- The reverse direction, "which organizations is user Y in, with what role", runs
-- at the start of EVERY request (row-level security). Covering index: the
-- membership lookup is answered from the index alone (index-only scan).
CREATE INDEX organization_members_user_idx
  ON organization_members (user_id, organization_id) INCLUDE (role);

CREATE TRIGGER organization_members_set_updated_at
  BEFORE UPDATE ON organization_members
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.set_updated_at();


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Invariant: an organization always has at least one owner
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Not expressible as a CHECK (it spans rows), so it is a CONSTRAINT TRIGGER.
-- DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED: the check runs at COMMIT, so ownership can be
-- transferred in one transaction (promote the new owner, then demote/remove the
-- old one) without tripping on the intermediate state.
-- Deleting the whole organization is allowed: by commit time the organization row
-- is gone, so there is nothing left to protect.
CREATE FUNCTION app.organization_keeps_an_owner() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = ''
AS $$
BEGIN
  IF OLD.role = 'owner'
     AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.organizations o WHERE o.id = OLD.organization_id)
     AND NOT EXISTS (
       SELECT 1 FROM public.organization_members m
        WHERE m.organization_id = OLD.organization_id AND m.role = 'owner')
  THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'organization % must keep at least one owner', OLD.organization_id
      USING ERRCODE = 'check_violation',
            HINT = 'Promote another member to owner before removing or demoting this one.';
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;
END
$$;

CREATE CONSTRAINT TRIGGER organization_members_keep_an_owner
  AFTER UPDATE OF role OR DELETE ON organization_members
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.organization_keeps_an_owner();
