NEXT: Task 1.3 critique via fresh subagent given ONLY schema SQL+SDL (not the doc/conversation); user writes own 500–750 word analysis. Gotcha: on Windows, TaskStop on a backgrounded `npm run db:serve` leaves the node child orphaned (still holding lock/port) — kill the PID recorded in api/.pglite.lock with `taskkill //PID <pid> //F`. Query plans verified on 24k-task seed under RLS: Q1 uses tasks_open_assigned_due_idx, Q2 keyset row-compare in tasks_board_idx index cond (11 buffers), Q3 GROUPING SETS single MixedAggregate, label filter planner picks direction by selectivity (rare 20 buffers / common 269 / correlated worst case 8.5k). Kysely Migrator has `disableTransactions` (for CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY).
**Findings to apply in Part 1:** RLS policies must use `nullif(current_setting('app.x', true), '')` — after first tx-local set_config a GUC reads '' (not NULL) and ''::int throws (verified). Kysely Migrator wraps the batch in one tx → no CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in migrations (mention in 1.2 migration strategy). Keyset cursors on timestamptz: JS Date loses µs precision — encode cursors as text or use id (uuidv7, PG18 built-in) to avoid skipped/duplicated rows.
**Company context (per user, 2026-11-17):** the Compliance Foundry group runs three companies — Compliance Foundry, Comperis Cybersecurity, Fixpliance AI — used (at user's request) in 0002_tenancy.sql as the example for why users↔organizations is many-to-many. Reuse it in 1.2 data-model rationale. User's employer (SysCloud) deliberately NOT named in repo files.
**Company stack (per user, 2026-11-11):** Compliance Foundry uses Sequelize (Node) and SQLAlchemy (Python) in production — weigh stack fit when choosing the query layer. Spec mandates Node for the API, so SQLAlchemy is out for code.
**Verified by spike 2026-11-11:** PGlite 0.5.x ships Postgres 18 (not 17); default user is superuser (bypasses RLS → need SET LOCAL ROLE); Sequelize v6 + stock `pg` works against PGlite via `@electric-sql/pglite-socket` (pool max 1), incl. transactions, RLS, Umzug running .sql files.
**Gotcha found 2026-11-16 (Kysely/raw `pg` path):** node-postgres parses DATE into a local-midnight JS Date → on this IST machine `2026-11-05` came back as `2026-11-04T18:30Z` (off-by-one-day for due dates and keyset cursors); int8 counts come back as strings. Fix once: `pg.types.setTypeParser(1082, v => v)` and int8 → Number (or `::int`). Drizzle's `date()` (string mode) + `count()` avoid both by default.

- **Prompt:** the exact brief I gave it is recorded at the top of [docs/part1/ai-critique.md](docs/part1/ai-critique.md).
- **Length:** it wrote about 3,600 words, beyond the 1,800–2,800 it was asked for.

## What it found (titles only, no verdicts from me)

| Area | Findings (severity) |
|---|---|
| N+1 | **N1** per-card lookups on the board, about 1,500 queries (High) · **N2** per-column pagination can't be batched simply, and page size `first` has no maximum (High) · **N3** activity timeline lookups and unbounded summary lists (Med) |
| Consistency | **C1** a category change rewrites `completed_at` with no history (Med) · **C2** race between a category change and a task move (Med) · **C3** card-order keys can collide and have no length limit (Med) · **C4** two owners leaving at once can leave an org with no owner (Low) · **C5** no protection against lost concurrent edits (Med) · **C6** former members vanish from history (Med) |
| Scale (100x) | **S1** the default sort and the summary scan the whole project (High) · **S2** row-level security blocks some index-only reads (Med) · **S3** org-wide operations run as huge single transactions (Med) · **S4** extra write work on drags and edits (Low) |
| Security | **SEC1** members can be added without consent: email enumeration and profile harvesting (High) · **SEC2** comment edit and moderation gaps (Med) · **SEC3** a privileged trigger runs before the RLS check (Low) · **SEC4** smaller hardening gaps (Low) |
| Indexes | **I1** columns referencing users have no index (Med) · **I2** status-wide maintenance can't use the partial board index (Low) |

## Next: your analysis (500–750 words)

The brief asks three things: do you agree with the critique, what did it miss, and what would you fix first and why? This is the part graded as *your* judgment, so here's how I suggest we split it:

- **A (recommended):** you write your take first, even as rough bullet notes. I then:
  - check each of your claims against the code and the measured query plans;
  - point out anything I can disprove;
  - tighten the wording and get it into the word range.

  The analysis stays yours.
- **B:** I first fact-check every critique finding against the code, the tests and the measured plans from 1.2, marking which claims hold and which don't. That's more evidence, but your analysis would then lean on my verdicts.

Some of the critique's claims can be checked against evidence we already have. I'm holding that back unless you ask, so it doesn't steer your view.

Once your analysis is done, your "fix first" priorities become schema v2: a new `0006_…` migration plus a changelog.

-- "My open tasks / my overdue tasks" across all projects and organizations. Partial:

# Verification of the AI Critique

**What this is:** a point-by-point check of [`ai-critique.md`](ai-critique.md) against the schema v1 code, Postgres semantics and measurements. It is evidence for the authors' assessment in [`critique-analysis.md`](critique-analysis.md), not that assessment itself.

**Method:**
- **Reading:** every finding's file and line references were checked against the code at `schema-v1`. All the spot-checked references were accurate.
- **Probes:** 14 probes ran on a 20,000-task seed (4,000 cards per status), mostly as `app_user` with row-level security on, using `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and direct reads and writes.
- **Reasoning:** PGlite is a single database session, so the three race-condition findings (C2, C3, C4) can't be reproduced on it. They were checked against Postgres's documented locking and visibility rules instead.

## Scoreboard

| Result | Findings |
|---|---|
| **Confirmed** | 16 of 19: N1, N2, N3, C1, C2 (reasoned), C3 (reasoned), C5, C6, S1, S3, S4, SEC1, SEC2, SEC3, I1, I2 |
| **Partly correct** | 3: **S2** (half refuted by measurement), **C4** (the race is real, but the scenario given can't happen), **SEC4** (all three gaps are real, but one proposed fix doesn't work) |
| **Wrong** | 0 |
| Already noted in our own 1.2 doc | S4 (rank updates aren't cheap in-place "HOT" updates; counter contention), S1 (summary cost only), S3 (per-row write policies, bulk cost only) |
| Wrong comments in our own code that it caught | `0005` "used in every policy" (write policies don't use the pattern) · `0003` "answered from the index alone" (not true under row-level security) · `0003` "board index" for status-wide updates (it's partial) · `0003` "with a due date" (no such condition) |

## Finding by finding

Where I'd rate severity differently from the critique, the critique's rating is shown first, then mine.

| ID | Verdict | Evidence | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **N1** Per-card lookups | ✅ Correct, as an implementation risk. It also adds a point we hadn't stated: batched queries still run *one after another* on the request's single connection | SDL shape; `withUserContext` holds one connection per request | High. Already planned: per-request DataLoaders (1.2 §2.4) |
| **N2** Per-column pages; no limit on `first` | ✅ No maximum anywhere in the SDL. `WHERE status_id = ANY(…)` can't apply a per-column `LIMIT`, so the `LATERAL` form is the right one | sdl:135-136, 192, 228, 268, 270, 532 | High. A cap of 100 and depth/cost limits are planned in the API layer (tech-stack doc), not in the schema |
| **N3** Timeline lookups; unbounded lists | ✅ 11 activity types; comments and activity are separate connections, so a merged timeline can't share one cursor | sdl:381-479 | Medium |
| **C1** Category change rewrites `completed_at` | ✅ **Demonstrated.** Done → started → completed changed a task's `completed_at` from `…31.248Z` to `…32.464Z`, and its history stayed at 2 rows | Probe C1 | Medium (agree) |
| **C2** Category copy races with task moves | ✅ **Reasoned.** A category UPDATE takes `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`; the FK check takes `FOR KEY SHARE`, which doesn't conflict with it. The trigger's plain SELECT reads the old category, and the propagation's snapshot misses the uncommitted move. The proposed `FOR SHARE` does conflict with `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, so the fix is correct, and it must run as SECURITY DEFINER | Postgres row-lock conflict table | Medium → **Low** (needs an admin edit at the same moment as a move; the critique itself says "rare") |
| **C3** Rank collisions; no length limit | ✅ **Reasoned.** There's no unique constraint, and ranks are computed before any lock. A fractional key can't be generated between two equal keys. A B-tree entry is capped at about 2.7 kB (a third of a page), which takes about 2,600 drops into the same gap | `0003` rank column; Part 2 `moveTask` must handle this | Medium → **Low–Medium** (duplicates are realistic; the length limit needs automation) |
| **C4** Organization left with no owner | ⚠️ **Race real, scenario wrong.** "A removes B while B leaves" deletes the *same* row: the second DELETE waits on the row lock, then finds the row gone and affects 0 rows, so no zero-owner state results. The real race involves *different* owner rows: A and B both leave at once, or each demotes the other. Each deferred check then still sees the other's row. The fix (lock the organization row) is correct | Reasoned from row-lock and visibility rules | Low (agree) |
| **C5** Lost concurrent edits | ✅ No version column and no expected-version input. `CONFLICT` is declared but unused | sdl:17, 721-728 | Medium (agree) |
| **C6** Former members vanish from history | ✅ **Demonstrated.** After Carol left, her comment's `author_id` was still stored, but the author resolved to **NULL**. The assignee history entry holding her id also resolved to NULL, so it reads the same as a genuine "was unassigned" entry | Probe C6 | Medium (agree). A real correctness bug |
| **S1** Default sort and summary scan the project | ✅ **Demonstrated.** `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50` read all **20,000 rows** and sorted them (422 pages) to return 50 | Probe S1 | High (agree). It's the *default* order of `Project.tasks` |
| **S2** Row-level security blocks index shortcuts | ⚠️ **Half right.** *Index-only counts:* confirmed. The owner's count uses an index-only scan (79 pages, 0 table fetches); with row-level security on it needs a bitmap heap scan (**472 pages**), because `organization_id` isn't in the index. *Cursor pages:* **refuted.** `ROW(rank, id) > ROW(…)` is part of the index lookup under row-level security (11 pages, 2,000 cards deep), and `text_gt/lt` and `uuid_gt/lt` are marked `leakproof = true` | Probes S2a, S2b | Medium → **Low–Medium** (only the counting half holds) |
| **S3** Organization-scale single transactions | ✅ The plan shows `app.has_organization_role(organization_id, 'member')` checked *per row* in bulk updates, next to the once-per-query check for reads. Cascading deletes queue every AFTER-trigger event in memory | Probe S3 | Medium (agree) |
| **S4** Extra writes on hot paths | ✅ The non-HOT rank updates were already in 1.2. New: `updated_at` changes on every drag, and `status_snapshot()` is computed even when the status didn't change | `0003` tasks_30, `0004` VALUES | Low (agree) |
| **SEC1** Members added without consent | ✅ **Demonstrated.** An Acme admin added Globex's owner as a viewer, and an Acme member could then read that person's email | Probe SEC1 | High (agree). A privacy issue, not a breach of another tenant's data |
| **SEC2** Comment edit and moderation gaps | ✅ **Demonstrated, all three:** an admin rewrote a member's comment (1 row); the author un-deleted it after moderation (1 row); the body stays stored after deletion | Probe SEC2 | Medium (agree) |
| **SEC3** Privileged trigger runs before the security check | ✅ **Demonstrated.** An Acme member inserting into Globex's project got `status 01a1ed6e…f6ef does not belong to project …`, which is Globex's real Todo status id. An archived or non-existent project gives a different message, so the error tells live projects apart from others | Probe SEC3 | Low (agree). Needs raw database errors to reach clients |
| **SEC4** Hardening gaps | ⚠️ **(a) Archived projects writable:** confirmed (a task in an archived project updated, 1 row). **(b) Future `app` functions callable:** confirmed, but **the proposed fix fails**. After `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA app REVOKE …`, a new function was *still* executable by `app_user`, because per-schema defaults can only *add* privileges. The global form (no `IN SCHEMA`) works. **(c) Id existence leak:** confirmed (`23505 … "tasks_pkey"`), but it needs an id the attacker already knows | Probes SEC4a/b/c | Low (agree) |
| **I1** User reference columns unindexed | ✅ `projects.created_by`, `tasks.created_by`, `task_comments.author_id` and `task_activities.actor_id` have no index (`organization_members.user_id` does) | Probe I1 (catalog) | Medium (agree) if account deletion is a feature |
| **I2** Status-wide work can't use the partial board index | ✅ Without a `deleted_at` condition the board index can't be used: a sequential scan removed **16,040** rows to find 4,000 | Probe I2 | Low (agree) |

## Answers to the critique's open questions

| Question | Answer from the design |
|---|---|
| Isolation level? | READ COMMITTED (Kysely's default; `withUserContext` sets none), so C2 and C4 apply as reasoned |
| Which role does the pool log in as? | The owner role (a superuser on PGlite). Requests drop to `app_user` inside `withUserContext`. **Any query outside it bypasses row-level security entirely**, so Part 2 must make that wrapper the only way to reach the database |
| Do raw database errors reach clients? | Not by design: GraphQL Yoga masks unexpected errors. That reduces SEC3 to its lock-contention part |
| Is account deletion a feature? | Not yet. I1 becomes urgent the day it is. Today a sole owner can't delete their account (intended) |
| Can viewers be assignees? | Currently yes (the foreign key allows any member). That's a product decision the schema didn't make explicitly |
| Retention for `task_activities`? | None yet. 1.2 names it the first candidate for partitioning |
| Are `text_gt` / `text_lt` leakproof? | **Yes**, verified on Postgres 18. That's why half of S2 doesn't hold |

# Part 1: System design

## Task 1.1: Data model (schema v1)

| Deliverable                   | Where                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| GraphQL type definitions      | [`schema.graphql`](schema.graphql): the full platform API                                                                                                                                |
| SQL `CREATE TABLE` statements | [`api/db/migrations/`](../../api/db/migrations/): five commented migration files, one concern each (listed below)                                                                        |
| Evidence that it works        | [`api/test/schema.test.ts`](../../api/test/schema.test.ts): 22 tests on real PostgreSQL 18, covering integrity, history, tenant isolation, roles, and the GraphQL↔Postgres enum contract |

### The five migrations

| Migration                        | Contents                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `0001_foundation.sql`            | Request role `app_user`, `app` schema, `current_user_id()`, `updated_at` trigger                                                          |
| `0002_tenancy.sql`               | `users`, `organizations`, `organization_settings`, `organization_members` (role enum, "always one owner" rule)                            |
| `0003_projects_and_tasks.sql`    | `projects`, `task_statuses` (custom per project, with a fixed category), `labels`, `tasks`, `task_labels`, and their indexes and triggers |
| `0004_comments_and_activity.sql` | `task_comments`; `task_activities` (append-only history, written by triggers)                                                             |
| `0005_access_control.sql`        | Column-level grants and row-level security policies, with the permission matrix                                                           |

**Schema v1 is frozen** (git tag `schema-v1`): the Task 1.3 critique reviews exactly this version, and fixes ship as new migrations (`0006_…`).

## Task 1.2: Technical documentation

[`technical-design.md`](technical-design.md) covers data model rationale and an entity-relationship diagram, query patterns (with verified query plans), indexing and performance, multi-tenancy isolation, and migration strategy.

## Task 1.3: AI critique and analysis

| Deliverable                    | Where                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| AI critique (raw, unedited)    | [`ai-critique.md`](ai-critique.md): an independent agent that read only the six schema files. Includes its exact prompt |
| Our assessment (500–750 words) | `critique-analysis.md`: _pending_                                                                                       |

name: compliance-foundry-take-home
description: "Compliance Foundry Senior Full-Stack (IC4/IC5) take-home — multi-tenant PM platform; schema/docs/critique, GraphQL API + React board, RFC; AI transcript is graded"
metadata:

  type: project
  originSessionId: 13bf4539-ab88-417f-9f03-71d2a332ad4a
  modified: 2026-11-18T06:27:59.924Z
---

User is doing the Compliance Foundry Senior Full-Stack take-home. Spec: `E:\Compliance Foundry Assignment\Senior Full-Stack Developer — Take-Home Technical Assessment.md`.
Parts: 1.1 GraphQL + Postgres schema, 1.2 tech doc (2–3 pp), 1.3 AI critique + user's OWN analysis (500–750 words), 2.1 Node GraphQL API (+200–300 word rationale), 2.2 React TS task board (+200–300 words), 3.1 RFC (2–3 pp). Complete unedited AI transcript + prompting-strategy commentary is a graded deliverable. Work started 2026-11-06; deadline is 7 days from assignment (exact date unconfirmed).

**Why:** evaluators grade how the user prompts, iterates and validates AI output, so process visibility matters as much as output.
**How to apply:** Agreed workflow: clear doubts → finalize tech stack → execute phase by phase per the doc; wait for the user's go-ahead before starting each phase. Related: [[user-senior-engineer]], [[code-comments-rule]]

**Decisions agreed 2026-11-06 (all my proposed defaults accepted):**
- Organization == workspace (single tenant entity); use the word "organization" everywhere.
- Part 1 SQL = real migrations; Part 2 implements the board subset on it.
- Schema v1 frozen for the 1.3 critique; v2 applies prioritized fixes + changelog.
- Auth: seeded users + signed JWT/dev header + "view as user" switcher; no real login.
- Board drag-and-drop mutation is `moveTask(input: {id, statusId, afterTaskId?, beforeTaskId?})` w/ optimistic UI (renamed 2026-11-16 from `updateTaskStatus`, which in the 1.1 SDL edits a status *definition*); Kanban w/ filter bar + per-column cursor pagination (`TaskStatus.tasks`).
- Focused tests (tenant isolation, pagination, filters, UI states). Seed: 2–3 orgs, ~10 users all roles, one ~2,500-task project.
- Tight production-quality slice, avoid sprawl (4–5h spirit).
- Git repo initialized (main); commit after each phase. `gh` not installed → user pushes to GitHub.
- 1.3 critique via a fresh unanchored subagent; user writes own analysis, I review.
- Don't email assessor; keep assumptions section in README.
Env: Node 24.12, npm 10.9, Docker installed but engine not running, no pnpm/psql/gh.

**Stack FINALIZED 2026-11-16** (rationale in repo `docs/tech-stack-choice.md` — keep it in sync if anything changes): PGlite (via pglite-socket + stock `pg`, pool max 1; DATABASE_URL for real PG) · hand-written .sql migrations + Kysely (Migrator + kysely-codegen) · GraphQL Yoga SDL-first (user knows PostGraphile from current employer — rejected as DB-first generator) · graphql-codegen · DataLoader · jose · zod 4 · Vite + React 19 · Apollo Client 4 · URL-param filters, no global store · Tailwind 4 / dnd-kit / Recharts 3 · Vitest + RTL · npm workspaces api/ web/ docs/.
**Progress:** 2026-11-16 scaffold committed (9f463c2): api/ workspace, PGlite+socket (maxConnections 1), pg parsers, Kysely Migrator over .sql (import from `kysely/migration` in 0.29), codegen w/ --verify, 11 DB tests, CI (actions v7), CLAUDE.md. TS pinned 6.0.x (typescript-eslint <6.1). `npm run check` is the gate. 2026-11-16: Part 1.1 drafted — migrations 0001–0005 (+0004 cascade fix), docs/part1/schema.graphql, docs/part1/README.md, src/db/request-context.ts (withUserContext), test/schema.test.ts (22 tests; 33 total green). Committed b6d9c74 + tag `schema-v1` (2026-11-17). 1.2 committed f58bcb9 (trimmed to ~1,780 words, option A). db:serve committed 8bce168: dev DB on 127.0.0.1:54320, db/user/pass postgres (unchecked), data-dir lock api/.pglite.lock. 1.3 raw critique committed 42aaa46 (docs/part1/ai-critique.md, verbatim, prettier-ignored, prompt in header; agent verified to have read only the 6 schema files; ~3,600 words — overshot its 1,800–2,800 budget). NEXT: user writes docs/part1/critique-analysis.md (500–750 words, their own judgment); I offered a claim-by-claim fact-check only if they ask. Known evidence relevant to their analysis (don't volunteer unasked): S2's leakproof claim is contradicted by the 1.2 measured plan (ROW(rank,id) was an Index Cond under RLS, 11 buffers). Then schema v2 = 0006+ migration with prioritized fixes + changelog. Gotcha: on Windows, TaskStop on a backgrounded `npm run db:serve` leaves the node child orphaned (still holding lock/port) — kill the PID recorded in api/.pglite.lock with `taskkill //PID <pid> //F`. Query plans verified on 24k-task seed under RLS: Q1 uses tasks_open_assigned_due_idx, Q2 keyset row-compare in tasks_board_idx index cond (11 buffers), Q3 GROUPING SETS single MixedAggregate, label filter planner picks direction by selectivity (rare 20 buffers / common 269 / correlated worst case 8.5k). Kysely Migrator has `disableTransactions` (for CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY).
**Findings to apply in Part 1:** RLS policies must use `nullif(current_setting('app.x', true), '')` — after first tx-local set_config a GUC reads '' (not NULL) and ''::int throws (verified). Kysely Migrator wraps the batch in one tx → no CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in migrations (mention in 1.2 migration strategy). Keyset cursors on timestamptz: JS Date loses µs precision — encode cursors as text or use id (uuidv7, PG18 built-in) to avoid skipped/duplicated rows.
**Company context (per user, 2026-11-17):** the Compliance Foundry group runs three companies — Compliance Foundry, Comperis Cybersecurity, Fixpliance AI — used (at user's request) in 0002_tenancy.sql as the example for why users↔organizations is many-to-many. Reuse it in 1.2 data-model rationale. User's employer (SysCloud) deliberately NOT named in repo files.
**Company stack (per user, 2026-11-11):** Compliance Foundry uses Sequelize (Node) and SQLAlchemy (Python) in production — weigh stack fit when choosing the query layer. Spec mandates Node for the API, so SQLAlchemy is out for code.
**Verified by spike 2026-11-11:** PGlite 0.5.x ships Postgres 18 (not 17); default user is superuser (bypasses RLS → need SET LOCAL ROLE); Sequelize v6 + stock `pg` works against PGlite via `@electric-sql/pglite-socket` (pool max 1), incl. transactions, RLS, Umzug running .sql files.
**Gotcha found 2026-11-16 (Kysely/raw `pg` path):** node-postgres parses DATE into a local-midnight JS Date → on this IST machine `2026-11-05` came back as `2026-11-04T18:30Z` (off-by-one-day for due dates and keyset cursors); int8 counts come back as strings. Fix once: `pg.types.setTypeParser(1082, v => v)` and int8 → Number (or `::int`). Drizzle's `date()` (string mode) + `count()` avoid both by default.

I've checked all 19 findings and committed the report as `610a6d3`: [docs/part1/critique-verification.md](docs/part1/critique-verification.md). **16 hold up, 3 are partly correct, and none are wrong.**

## How I checked
- **Line references:** I matched the critique's citations against the code at `schema-v1`. Every one I checked was accurate.
- **14 probes on a 20,000-task database:** mostly run as a normal member with row-level security on. Where a claim could be shown by running something, I ran it.
- **Race conditions (C2, C3, C4):** these can't be reproduced, because PGlite allows only one database session at a time. I checked them against Postgres's documented locking rules instead.

## Where the AI was wrong (the 3 partial findings)

| Finding | What holds | What doesn't |
|---|---|---|
| **S2** row-level security vs indexes | Per-status counts can no longer be answered from the index alone: 79 pages become 472 | The claim that cursor paging degrades is false. The cursor condition is still used in the index lookup (11 pages, 2,000 cards deep), because the comparison functions involved are marked `leakproof` on Postgres 18 |
| **C4** organization left with no owner | The race is real when two *different* owners leave, or demote each other, at the same moment | The scenario it describes ("A removes B while B leaves") targets the *same* row. The second delete waits, then finds nothing to delete, so that scenario can't happen |
| **SEC4b** new functions callable by the API role | The gap is real | Its proposed fix doesn't work. After the per-schema revoke, a new function was *still* executable by the API role. The global form of the command works |

## Real bugs it caught, now demonstrated
- **C6:** after a member leaves, their comments show no author. A history entry recording that the task was assigned to them reads exactly like "was unassigned", so the history now says something false.
- **C1:** an admin switching Done → started → completed overwrote a task's real completion time, and no history row was written.
- **SEC1:** an Acme admin added Globex's owner to Acme without their consent. Acme members could then read that person's email.
- **SEC2:** an admin rewrote a member's comment, and the author un-deleted it after it was moderated.
- **S1:** the default task list read all 20,000 rows to return 50, because nothing indexes `created_at`.
- **Our own code comments:** it caught four that were wrong, including "answered from the index alone" and "used in every policy".

**One requirement for Part 2,** from its open questions: any query that runs *outside* `withUserContext` skips row-level security entirely. The API must allow no other path to the database.

The three questions are still yours: do you agree, what did it miss, and what would you fix first and why. You now have evidence for the "where it was wrong" part.

# Assessment of the AI Critique

_Drafted by Claude at the author's request, from the evidence in [`critique-verification.md`](critique-verification.md)._

## Do I agree?

Largely, yes. Of the critique's 19 findings, 16 held up when checked against the code and 14 probes on a 20,000-task dataset, and none was wrong outright. Its strength is that it reasons from Postgres semantics rather than generic advice. The status-category race (C2) hinges on `FOR KEY SHARE` not conflicting with `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, and its proposed fix is correct. It also caught four comments in our migrations that overstate what the code does: the kind of drift reviewers rarely notice.

Where I disagree:

- **S2 (cursor pages under row-level security) is half wrong.** Measurement shows the cursor comparison stays part of the index lookup under row-level security (11 pages read, 2,000 cards deep), because Postgres 18 marks the text and uuid comparison functions as `leakproof`. The critique correctly labelled this as inference. The half that does hold (counts can't be served from the index alone) is a one-line fix.
- **C4's race is real, but the scenario it gives isn't.** Two transactions removing the *same* membership row simply queue on that row's lock. The real race needs two *different* owners leaving at the same moment.
- **SEC4b's fix doesn't work.** A per-schema `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` can add privileges but never revoke them. The same mistake appeared while `0001` was being written and was caught by running it, a reminder that plausible-looking DDL has to be executed, not just read.
- **Two severities are too high.** N1 is a risk in how resolvers get written, not a schema defect, and DataLoaders were already planned. C2 needs an admin to edit a status at the same moment someone moves a task into it, so it's Low rather than Medium.

## What it missed

1. **Row-level security is opt-in, not the default.** The critique asked which role the pool logs in as, but didn't draw the conclusion. The API connects as the schema owner, and only `withUserContext` drops privileges, so one forgotten wrapper exposes every tenant's data. In production the API should log in as a non-owner role, so row-level security applies by default; the owner role is for migrations only.
2. **Timestamp cursors lose precision between the database and JavaScript.** Postgres stores timestamps to the microsecond; a JavaScript `Date` keeps only milliseconds. Comment and history timelines paginate on `(created_at, id)`, so a cursor that passes through `Date` can skip or repeat rows. A review of the schema alone can't see this, because it lives in the driver. Cursors must be encoded as text, or use the time-ordered `id` alone.
3. **One transaction per request ties response time to connection time.** Each GraphQL request holds a pooled connection for its whole duration, because the security context lives in that transaction. At 100x, pool size rather than CPU becomes the concurrency limit. Resolvers must not wait on anything other than the database inside the transaction, and PgBouncer in transaction mode is the way to scale (it's compatible with `SET LOCAL`).

## What I'd fix first, and why

I ranked by damage × likelihood, divided by the cost of the fix:

1. **Forbid changing the category of a status that still has tasks** (C1, C2, part of I2). One trigger removes a whole class of silent corruption: completion times rewritten with no history, the race against task moves, and full-project rescans. Admins instead create a new status and move the tasks, which records history for each one. It's the cheapest fix with the biggest integrity gain.
2. **Stop the API role from inserting memberships directly** (SEC1). Any signed-up user can exploit this privacy hole today. An invitation flow (a token with an expiry, accepted by the invitee) replaces it.
3. **Build Part 2 so the N+1 and paging problems can't happen:**
   - per-request DataLoaders and one `LATERAL` query for all the columns' pages;
   - `first` capped at 100;
   - card order computed server-side under a per-column lock (C3);
   - database errors hidden from clients (SEC3), with a membership check *before* the privileged trigger does anything.
4. **Cheap index fixes:** add `INCLUDE (organization_id)` to the board index so per-status counts come from the index alone (S2), and serve the default task order from the existing `(project_id, number)` index (S1).
5. **Next:** keep former members' names in history by marking memberships as left rather than deleting them (C6), and route comment moderation through a privileged function that clears the body (SEC2). Both are real bugs, but neither touches the board, and both need product decisions first.

**Deliberately deferred:** version columns against lost edits (C5), until a collaborative description editor exists; indexes for user-reference columns (I1), until account deletion is a feature.

# Assessment of the AI Critique

_Drafted by Claude at the author's request, from the evidence in [`critique-verification.md`](critique-verification.md)._

## Do I agree?

Largely, yes. Of the critique's 19 findings, 16 held up when checked against the code and 14 probes on a 20,000-task dataset, and none was wrong outright. Its strength is that it reasons from Postgres semantics rather than generic advice. The status-category race (C2) hinges on `FOR KEY SHARE` not conflicting with `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, and its proposed fix is correct. It also caught four migration comments that overstate what the code does.

Where I disagree:

- **S2 (cursor pages under row-level security) is half wrong.** Measurement shows the cursor comparison stays part of the index lookup under row-level security (11 pages read, 2,000 cards deep), because Postgres 18 marks the text and uuid comparison functions as `leakproof`. The half that holds (counts can't come from the index alone) is a one-line fix.
- **C4's race is real, but the scenario it gives isn't.** Two transactions removing the _same_ membership row simply queue on that row's lock. The real race needs two _different_ owners leaving at the same moment.
- **SEC4b's fix doesn't work.** A per-schema `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` can add privileges but never revoke them. The same mistake appeared while `0001` was being written and was caught by running it, a reminder that plausible-looking DDL has to be executed, not just read.
- **Two severities are too high.** N1 is a risk in how resolvers get written, not a schema defect, and DataLoaders were already planned. C2 needs an admin to edit a status at the same moment someone moves a task into it, so it's Low rather than Medium.

## What it missed

1. **Row-level security is opt-in, not the default.** The critique asked which role the pool logs in as, but didn't draw the conclusion. The API connects as the schema owner, and only `withUserContext` drops privileges, so one forgotten wrapper exposes every tenant's data. In production the API should log in as a non-owner role, so row-level security applies by default; the owner role is for migrations only.
2. **Timestamp cursors lose precision between the database and JavaScript.** Postgres stores timestamps to the microsecond; a JavaScript `Date` keeps only milliseconds. Comment and history timelines paginate on `(created_at, id)`, so a cursor that passes through `Date` can skip or repeat rows. A schema-only review can't see this; it lives in the driver. Cursors must be encoded as text, or use the time-ordered `id` alone.
3. **One transaction per request ties response time to connection time.** Each GraphQL request holds a pooled connection for its whole duration, because the security context lives in that transaction. At 100x, pool size rather than CPU becomes the concurrency limit. Resolvers must not wait on anything other than the database inside the transaction; PgBouncer in transaction mode is the scaling path.

1. **Forbid changing the category of a status that still has tasks** (C1, C2, part of I2). One trigger removes a whole class of silent corruption: completion times rewritten with no history, the race against task moves, and full-project rescans. -- queue on that project's row lock for the rest of their transaction, so numbers
-- are gap-free and never duplicated (a rolled-back insert does leave a gap).
CREATE FUNCTION app.tasks_before_insert() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = ''
AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE public.projects p
     SET task_counter = p.task_counter + 1
   WHERE p.id = NEW.project_id
     AND p.organization_id = NEW.organization_id
     AND p.archived_at IS NULL
  RETURNING p.task_counter INTO NEW.number;

  IF NEW.number IS NULL THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'project % does not exist in organization % or is archived',
      NEW.project_id, NEW.organization_id
      USING ERRCODE = 'foreign_key_violation';
  END IF;

  IF NEW.status_id IS NULL THEN
    -- The project's default status; if none is flagged, its first open column.
    SELECT s.id INTO NEW.status_id
      FROM public.task_statuses s
     WHERE s.project_id = NEW.project_id
       AND s.category NOT IN ('completed', 'canceled')
     ORDER BY s.is_default DESC, s.position, s.id
     LIMIT 1;
  END IF;

  RETURN NEW;
END
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER tasks_10_before_insert
  BEFORE INSERT ON tasks
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.tasks_before_insert();

-- 2) Keep status_category and completed_at in sync with status_id.
-- Runs as the invoking user (no DEFINER needed): it only reads a status the user
-- can already see. A status from another project raises here, with a clearer
-- message than the composite FK would give.
CREATE FUNCTION app.tasks_sync_status() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql SET search_path = ''
AS $$
DECLARE
  v_category public.status_category;
BEGIN
  SELECT s.category INTO v_category
    FROM public.task_statuses s
   WHERE s.id = NEW.status_id AND s.project_id = NEW.project_id;

  IF v_category IS NULL THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'status % does not belong to project %', NEW.status_id, NEW.project_id
      USING ERRCODE = 'foreign_key_violation';
  END IF;

  NEW.status_category := v_category;
  -- Entering 'completed' stamps completed_at; moving between two completed
  -- statuses keeps the original stamp; leaving 'completed' clears it.
  NEW.completed_at := CASE
    WHEN v_category <> 'completed' THEN NULL
    WHEN TG_OP = 'UPDATE' AND OLD.completed_at IS NOT NULL THEN OLD.completed_at
    ELSE pg_catalog.now()
  END;
  RETURN NEW;
END
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER tasks_20_sync_status
  BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF status_id ON tasks
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.tasks_sync_status();

CREATE TRIGGER tasks_30_set_updated_at
  BEFORE UPDATE ON tasks
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.set_updated_at();

-- 3) A status whose CATEGORY changes (e.g. an admin turns "QA" from started into
-- completed) re-syncs the denormalised copy on all of its tasks — the price of
-- the denormalisation, paid on a rare admin action instead of on every read.
-- SECURITY DEFINER: app_user has no UPDATE right on these trigger-owned columns.

-- =============================================================================
-- 0006_critique_fixes.sql — schema v2: the fixes prioritised in Task 1.3
-- =============================================================================
-- What: applies the "fix first" items from docs/part1/critique-analysis.md, plus
--       cheap hardening the verification confirmed. Every change cites its
--       finding ID in docs/part1/ai-critique.md; docs/part1/schema-changelog.md
--       lists them with what was deliberately deferred.
-- Why a new file: 0001–0005 are schema v1 (git tag schema-v1) and are never
--       edited. That includes four v1 comments the critique showed to be wrong,
--       corrected here instead:
--         * 0003 tasks_board_idx "counts per status … from the index alone":
--           false under row-level security until change 3 below.
--         * 0003 propagation "(project_id, status_id) = board index": the board
--           index is partial (live tasks only), so it never applied. The
--           propagation is removed by change 1.
--         * 0003 tasks_open_assigned_due_idx "with a due date": the index has no
--           due_date condition; it covers open, live, assigned tasks.
--         * 0005 "(SELECT app.fn()) … used in every policy": only READ policies
--           use it; write policies call has_organization_role() per row (S3,
--           deferred — single-row API writes make it negligible today).
-- =============================================================================


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 0) SEC4b — new functions are no longer executable by PUBLIC by default
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- The critique's proposed `… IN SCHEMA app` form cannot work (per-schema default
-- privileges only ADD to the global ones — verified). The global form covers every
-- function this migration role creates from now on, including those below.
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC;


-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 1) C1 / C2 / I2 — a status's category is fixed while any task uses it
-- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- v1 let an admin re-categorise a status and then re-synced every task in it.

# Schema Changelog

## v2: `0006_critique_fixes.sql` (2026-11-18)

Applies the "fix first" items from [`critique-analysis.md`](critique-analysis.md). Finding IDs refer to [`ai-critique.md`](ai-critique.md). v1 (`0001–0005`, git tag `schema-v1`) is unchanged; four of its comments that the critique showed to be wrong are corrected in the header of `0006`.

| Change | Finding | Verified by |
|---|---|---|
| A status's category can't change while any task (including soft-deleted ones) uses it. The v1 trigger that re-synced tasks after a category change is removed | C1, C2, I2 | Test: "…freezes the category of a used status" |
| The task trigger reads the category with `FOR SHARE` (as SECURITY DEFINER), so a concurrent move and a category change conflict instead of racing | C2 (the guard above would otherwise reopen it) | Reasoned from the Postgres lock conflict table; PGlite can't run concurrent sessions |
| The API role can no longer insert memberships (policy and grant removed). An invitation flow will replace it | SEC1 | Test: "adds people … only through privileged paths" |
| The board index gains `INCLUDE (organization_id)` | S2 | Measured: per-status count under row-level security is now an index-only scan (0 table fetches, 112 pages), down from a bitmap heap scan (472) |
| The insert trigger checks membership first, refusing before touching another tenant's project, with no ids in the message | SEC3 | Test: a cross-tenant insert gets `42501`, and the message has no Globex ids |
| The owner check locks the organization row before counting owners | C4 | Reasoned (concurrent sessions) |
| `CHECK (octet_length(rank) <= 255)` | C3 (key length) | Test |
| `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC` (global form) | SEC4b | Test: a function created later isn't executable by `app_user` |

## Handled in the API (Part 2), not the schema

| Finding | How |
|---|---|
| N1 per-card lookups | Per-request DataLoaders; `identifier` and `isOverdue` computed in the task query |
| N2 per-column pages; unbounded `first` | One `LATERAL` query for every column's page; `first` capped at 100 |
| C3 duplicate rank keys | `moveTask` computes keys server-side under a per-column `pg_advisory_xact_lock` |
| SEC3 error disclosure | GraphQL Yoga masks unexpected errors; database messages never reach clients |
| S1 default `CREATED_AT` order | Served from the existing `(project_id, number)` index; numbers are assigned in creation order |
| "Row-level security is opt-in" (from the analysis) | `withUserContext` is the only way resolvers reach the database |
| Timestamp cursor precision (from the analysis) | Cursors are encoded from text/uuid values, never round-tripped through JavaScript `Date` |

## Deferred, with reasons

| Finding | Why not yet |
|---|---|
| C6 former members vanish from history | Needs soft membership (`left_at`) and a product decision on what ex-members' profiles show |
| SEC2 comment moderation | Comments aren't part of the Part 2 board; needs a moderation function that clears the body |
| SEC1 follow-up: invitations | The direct path is closed; the invitation flow (token, expiry, accept) is a feature of its own |
| SEC4a archived projects writable | Archive checks in every write policy cost a per-row lookup; the API refuses writes to archived projects first |
| C5 lost concurrent edits | Matters once collaborative description editing exists |
| I1 user-reference indexes | Only needed once account deletion is a feature |
| N3 merged timeline, S3 bulk write cost, S4 drag overhead, SEC4c id existence | Low impact at current scale; recorded for the Part 3 RFC |

input.content:
# =============================================================================
# Task Board API — the GraphQL contract implemented in Part 2 (Task 2.1)
# =============================================================================
# What: the Task Board slice of the platform design in docs/part1/schema.graphql.
#       Every type, field and enum value here exists there with the same type, so
#       clients written against this API keep working as the rest of the design is
#       implemented (enforced by api/test/graphql-contract.test.ts).
# Not implemented yet (design only): comments, activity history, and the
#       configuration/membership mutations.
#
# Conventions (from the design):
#   * Lists that can grow are cursor connections: `first` (max 100) + `after`.
#   * Errors carry `extensions.code`: UNAUTHENTICATED, FORBIDDEN, NOT_FOUND,
#     BAD_USER_INPUT, CONFLICT. Unexpected errors are masked ("Unexpected error.").
#   * Objects outside the caller's organizations resolve to null / NOT_FOUND —
#     the API never confirms that another tenant's ids exist.
# =============================================================================

"An instant in time: ISO-8601 with offset, e.g. `2026-11-16T09:30:00Z`."
scalar DateTime

"A calendar date with no time or zone: `YYYY-MM-DD`."
scalar Date

enum OrganizationRole {
  VIEWER
  MEMBER
  ADMIN
  OWNER
}

enum TaskPriority {
  NONE
  LOW
  MEDIUM
  HIGH
  URGENT
}

enum StatusCategory {
  BACKLOG
  UNSTARTED
  STARTED
  COMPLETED
  CANCELED
}

enum SortDirection {
  ASC
  DESC
}

enum TaskSortField {
  "Manual board order. Only meaningful within one status column."
  RANK
  PRIORITY
  DUE_DATE
  "Newest first by default. Served from the per-project sequence number."
  CREATED_AT
  "The per-project sequence number (WEB-1, WEB-2, …)."
  NUMBER
}

"Cursor pagination state. Cursors are opaque; pass `endCursor` as `after`."
type PageInfo {
  hasNextPage: Boolean!
  endCursor: String
}

type User {
  id: ID!
  displayName: String!
  email: String!
  avatarUrl: String
}

"The signed-in user and their organizations."
type Viewer {
  user: User!
  memberships: [OrganizationMember!]!
}

type Organization {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
  slug: String!
  createdAt: DateTime!
  "The signed-in user's role here — drives which controls the UI shows."
  viewerRole: OrganizationRole!
  settings: OrganizationSettings!
  members(first: Int = 50, after: String): OrganizationMemberConnection!
  projects(includeArchived: Boolean = false, first: Int = 50, after: String): ProjectConnection!
  labels: [Label!]!
}

type OrganizationSettings {
  timezone: String!
  weekStartsOn: Int!
  membersCanCreateProjects: Boolean!
  updatedAt: DateTime!
}

type OrganizationMember {
  organization: Organization!
  user: User!
  role: OrganizationRole!
  joinedAt: DateTime!
}

type OrganizationMemberConnection {
  edges: [OrganizationMemberEdge!]!
  pageInfo: PageInfo!
}

type OrganizationMemberEdge {
  cursor: String!
  node: OrganizationMember!
}

type Project {
  id: ID!
  organization: Organization!
  key: String!
  name: String!
  description: String
  archivedAt: DateTime
  createdBy: User
  createdAt: DateTime!
  updatedAt: DateTime!
  "The board's columns, in display order."
  statuses: [TaskStatus!]!
  "All live tasks of the project, filtered and sorted. Default order: newest first."
  tasks(
    filter: TaskFilter
    orderBy: TaskOrder = { field: CREATED_AT, direction: DESC }
    first: Int = 50
    after: String
  ): TaskConnection!
  "Counts for the summary panel and charts, honouring the same filter as `tasks`."
  taskSummary(filter: TaskFilter): TaskSummary!
}

type ProjectConnection {
  edges: [ProjectEdge!]!
  pageInfo: PageInfo!
}

type ProjectEdge {
  cursor: String!
  node: Project!
}

"A customizable status (board column) of one project."
type TaskStatus {
  id: ID!
  project: Project!
  name: String!
  category: StatusCategory!
  color: String!
  position: Int!
  isDefault: Boolean!
  "This column's tasks, in board order by default; each column pages independently."
  tasks(
    filter: TaskFilter
    orderBy: TaskOrder = { field: RANK, direction: ASC }
    first: Int = 50
    after: String
  ): TaskConnection!
}

type Label {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
  color: String!
}

type Task {
  id: ID!
  "Human identifier: project key + number, e.g. `WEB-42`."
  identifier: String!
  number: Int!
  project: Project!
  title: String!
  description: String
  status: TaskStatus!
  priority: TaskPriority!
  assignee: User
  labels: [Label!]!
  dueDate: Date
  "Open (not COMPLETED/CANCELED) and due before today in the organization's time zone."
  isOverdue: Boolean!
  completedAt: DateTime
  createdBy: User
  createdAt: DateTime!
  updatedAt: DateTime!
}

type TaskConnection {
  edges: [TaskEdge!]!
  pageInfo: PageInfo!
}

type TaskEdge {
  cursor: String!
  node: Task!
}

"Filters combine with AND; values inside one list combine with OR."
input TaskFilter {
  statusIds: [ID!]
  statusCategories: [StatusCategory!]
  assigneeIds: [ID!]
  "Also (OR) match tasks with no assignee; on its own, matches unassigned tasks only."
  includeUnassigned: Boolean
  priorities: [TaskPriority!]
  labelIds: [ID!]
  dueDate: DateRange
  overdue: Boolean
}

"An inclusive date range; either end may be omitted."
input DateRange {
  from: Date
  to: Date
}

input TaskOrder {
  field: TaskSortField!
  direction: SortDirection! = ASC
}

"Aggregates over the live tasks matching a filter, computed in one SQL pass."
type TaskSummary {
  total: Int!
  overdue: Int!
  "One entry per status of the project, in column order — including zero counts."
  byStatus: [StatusCount!]!
  "One entry per priority, NONE → URGENT — including zero counts."
  byPriority: [PriorityCount!]!
  "Busiest first (top 50). The entry with `assignee: null` counts unassigned tasks."
  byAssignee: [AssigneeCount!]!
}

type StatusCount {
  status: TaskStatus!
  count: Int!
}

type PriorityCount {
  priority: TaskPriority!
  count: Int!
}

type AssigneeCount {
  assignee: User
  count: Int!
}

type Query {
  "The signed-in user. UNAUTHENTICATED without a valid token."
  viewer: Viewer!
  "An organization the viewer belongs to; null otherwise."
  organization(slug: String!): Organization
  project(id: ID!): Project

# Part 2: Full-Stack Implementation

## Task 2.1: Backend GraphQL API

| Deliverable | Where |
|---|---|
| GraphQL schema (type definitions) | [`api/src/graphql/schema.graphql`](../../api/src/graphql/schema.graphql) |
| Resolver implementation | [`api/src/graphql/resolvers.ts`](../../api/src/graphql/resolvers.ts), with SQL in [`api/src/repositories/tasks.ts`](../../api/src/repositories/tasks.ts) and batching in [`loaders.ts`](../../api/src/graphql/loaders.ts) |
| Tests | [`api/test/graphql.test.ts`](../../api/test/graphql.test.ts) (every result checked against SQL ground truth) and [`graphql-contract.test.ts`](../../api/test/graphql-contract.test.ts) |

Run it with `npm run setup` then `npm run dev`. GraphiQL is at http://localhost:4000/graphql, and http://localhost:4000/dev/users gives a token for every seeded user.

### Design decisions

**The contract comes first.** The SDL is a strict subset of the Part 1 design (a test enforces it), and GraphQL Code Generator types every resolver against it, so drift fails the build.

**Authorization is enforced by Postgres, not by memory.** Each GraphQL operation runs in one transaction as `app_user`, with the caller's id set, so row-level security filters every query. Resolvers get only that transaction; no unscoped database handle exists. Other tenants' ids return `null` or `NOT_FOUND`, never "forbidden", and database messages are masked.

**The query count is constant.** Per-request DataLoaders batch every relation. All board columns page in one `LATERAL` query, and `identifier` and `isOverdue` are computed in SQL. A test proves a board load issues the same number of queries for 5 or 50 cards per column. The summary is one `GROUPING SETS` pass.

**Pagination is keyset-based.** Cursors encode `(sort value, id)`, never timestamps, so JavaScript's millisecond precision can't skip rows. Sorts use index-friendly keys, with undated tasks last. `first` is capped at 100 and query depth at 10.

**`moveTask` is safe under concurrency.** The server computes a fractional rank between the neighbours while holding a per-column advisory lock, so concurrent drops can't produce the same key. A failed mutation rolls back entirely.

**Trade-off:** a transaction holds its connection for the whole operation, so resolvers may only wait on the database. The summary still scans the project on every request, which Part 3 addresses.

**The query count is constant.** Per-request DataLoaders batch every relation. All board columns page in one `LATERAL` query, and `identifier` and `isOverdue` are computed in SQL. A test proves a board load issues the same number of queries for 5 or 50 cards per column. The summary is one `GROUPING SETS` pass.

**Pagination is keyset-based.** Cursors encode `(sort value, id)`, never timestamps, so JavaScript's millisecond precision can't skip rows. Sorts use index-friendly keys, with undated tasks last. `first` is capped at 100 and query depth at 10.

**`moveTask` is safe under concurrency.** The server computes a fractional rank between the neighbours while holding a per-column advisory lock, so concurrent drops can't produce the same key. A failed mutation rolls back entirely.

**Trade-off:** a transaction holds its connection for the whole operation, so resolvers may only wait on the database. The summary still scans the project on every request, which Part 3 addresses.

## 1. Your critique analysis
[docs/part1/critique-analysis.md](docs/part1/critique-analysis.md) answers the brief's three questions:
- **Where I agree:** 16 of the 19 findings held up.
- **Where I disagree:** S2's claim about paging under row-level security (measurements refuted it), C4's scenario, and SEC4b's fix, which doesn't work.
- **What it missed:** three things. Row-level security only applies inside the per-request wrapper; timestamps lose precision in JavaScript; and one transaction per request makes pool size the concurrency limit.
- **What to fix first, in order.**

It opens with one line saying I drafted it at your request. It goes out under your name, so please read it and change anything you don't stand behind.

## 2. Schema v2
`0006_critique_fixes.sql` applies the fix-first list:
- a status's category is frozen while tasks use it, with a lock that prevents the race this would otherwise reopen;
- direct membership inserts are removed;
- the board index includes the organization id, so per-column counts now come from the index alone (measured: 112 pages read instead of 472);
- non-members are rejected before the privileged insert trigger runs;
- the owner check now locks, and card-order keys are capped in length.

[docs/part1/schema-changelog.md](docs/part1/schema-changelog.md) maps every finding to fixed, handled in the API, or deferred with a reason.

**My slip:** in a multi-line shell command, I briefly put the `schema-v2` tag on the wrong commit. I moved it; there's no remote, so nothing outside your machine saw it.

## 3. Task 2.1: the API
Every critique finding that applies to the API is addressed in the code:
- **Security:** every GraphQL operation runs in one transaction as the restricted database role, so row-level security filters everything. Resolvers have no other way to reach the database.
- **No N+1:** a test shows a board load issues the **same number of queries for 5 or 50 cards per column**.
- **Pagination:** cursors never contain timestamps, `first` is capped at 100 and query depth at 10.
- **`moveTask`:** the server computes the card's position under a per-column lock. A move by a viewer returns FORBIDDEN, and a stale board returns CONFLICT.

**Verified:**
- 54 tests pass; the API's results are compared with direct SQL.
- On the real server, the 2,500-task board loads in **76 ms** (PGlite, not a production number). Viewers get FORBIDDEN, and another tenant's project returns `null`.

**Two bugs found while testing:**
- `graphql` 17 got loaded twice under Vitest, which silently masked every intended error. Fixed in the test config; the real server was unaffected, which I confirmed live.
- My own miscount in the query-depth test.

**`npm audit`:** it flags 17 issues, all in development tooling. Production dependencies have 0.

**Try it:**
```
npm run setup    # migrate + demo data (already done on your machine)
npm run dev      # http://localhost:4000/graphql
```
Tokens for every demo user are at http://localhost:4000/dev/users. `db:serve` (DBeaver) and `npm run dev` can't run at the same time, because they share the database lock.

## Next: Task 2.2, the board UI
The plan is a new `web/` workspace using Vite, React 19, Apollo Client 4, Tailwind and dnd-kit:
- **Board:** Kanban columns with "load more", drag-and-drop that moves the card instantly and rolls back on error, and a "view as user" switcher.
- **Filters:** stored in the URL.
- **Summary:** stats panel with a priority chart (Recharts).
- **States:** loading, error and empty.

Starting Task 2.2. One gap in the API showed up while planning: **"load more" for a single column has no way to address one column**. Re-running the board query with an `after` cursor would apply that column's cursor to *every* column and corrupt their lists.

The fix is one small root field, `taskStatus(id)`, added to both the design SDL and the API. Apollo stores each column once, normalised by its id, so the board query and the per-column "load more" query then share one cached `tasks` list, and new pages simply append. I'll add it with a test.

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
  One exception, legend kept: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

# Reference palette

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic - **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and
re-run the validator. Nothing else changes.

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout - so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* ...only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:where(:not([data-theme="light"])) .viz-root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #f0efec;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #f0efec;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

Declare the dark values under both scopes as above - the media query covers
the OS setting; the `data-theme` scope covers the viewer's theme toggle,
which must win both ways (the `:not(...)` guard lets a light stamp beat
OS-dark; `:where()` keeps the media block below the toggle scope).

## Categorical palette

Both modes are selected. The dark column is the same eight hues stepped for the
dark surface, not a separate palette:

| Slot | Hue | Light | Dark |
|------|-----|-------|------|
| 1 | blue | `#2a78d6` | `#3987e5` |
| 2 | orange | `#eb6834` | `#d95926` |
| 3 | aqua | `#1baf7a` | `#199e70` |
| 4 | yellow | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 5 | magenta | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
| 6 | green | `#008300` | `#008300` |
| 7 | violet | `#6250d6` | `#9085e9` |
| 8 | red | `#e34948` | `#e66767` |

This order passes every hard gate in both modes on the default *adjacent*
pairlist (stacks, bars, lines): worst adjacent CVD Delta E 9.1 light / 8.4 dark
(OKLab ×100, >=8 target), worst adjacent normal-vision Delta E 19.6 light / 19.3
dark (>=15 floor). Under `--pairs all` (scatter, bubble, choropleth, small
multiples) the full eight cannot clear the floors - with all 28 pairs in
play no ordering can (the pairlist no longer depends on order), and
re-stepping is off the table by the documented-palette rule - so those
chart forms carry a series cap: **the first three slots validate all-pairs
in both modes** (worst pair CVD Delta E 9.2 light / 9.4 dark, normal-vision 24.0
light / 20.9 dark - clear of the CVD warn band). Past three, fold to "Other" or
facet: the fourth slot puts yellow and orange on screen
together, and that pair fails the all-pairs floors (normal-vision 13.7
light; CVD 4.8 dark). Three light-mode slots (magenta, yellow, aqua)
sit below 3:1 contrast on the light surface: the **relief rule** applies (ship
visible direct labels or the table view). The dark steps were chosen for the
dark band (OKLCH L ~ 0.48-0.67, >= 3:1 on the dark surface) and validated as a
set. (Ordering history: adopted July 2026 for its more harmonious opening -
the same eight hues and steps as its predecessor, re-ordered, zero hex
changes. The predecessor validated its first FOUR slots all-pairs, with its
dark run in the 6-8 CVD warn band, so secondary encoding was required there;
this order deliberately trades that fourth slot - yellow now sits beside orange -
for better-looking leading colors. Revisit the trade if yellow<->orange
confusion shows up in real charts with four or more series; undoing it is a
pure re-order. Light slot 7 has since been lightened, `#4a3aa7` -> `#6250d6`
(August 2026); the adjacent-pair figures above are unchanged by that move, the
non-adjacent blue<->violet pair now sits below both floors under `--pairs all`
(normal-vision 10.5, CVD 4.5 - inside the range the series cap already
excludes), and the order enumeration was run with the earlier value.) When you
swap in your own ramps, hold your palette to the full gate.

The slot **ordering** is the CVD-safety mechanism, not cosmetic - candidate
orderings were enumerated and only those clearing every adjacent gate in both
modes kept (see `color-formula.md` § Themes); this default is one of the
passing orders, picked among them for its opening colors. When you swap in
your brand's hues, do the same: run the validator on candidate orderings and
choose only among the passing ones.

## Sequential hue

Default single hue: **blue**, light->dark. When two sequential contexts appear at
once, the second takes the next categorical slot's hue (orange), each as its own
one-hue ramp.

| step | hex | step | hex | step | hex | step | hex |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | `#cde2fb` | 250 | `#86b6ef` | 400 | `#3987e5` | 550 | `#1c5cab` |
| 150 | `#b7d3f6` | 300 | `#6da7ec` | 450 | `#2a78d6` | 600 | `#184f95` |
| 200 | `#9ec5f4` | 350 | `#5598e7` | 500 | `#256abf` | 650 | `#104281` |
| | | | | | | 700 | `#0d366b` |

The full 100->700 range is for **sequential** encoding (continuous magnitude -
heatmaps, choropleths) where the lightest step means "near zero" and is allowed
to recede toward the surface. For an **ordinal** ramp (discrete ordered marks -
funnel stages, tiers - validated with `--ordinal`), the step nearest the surface
must still clear 2:1: on light, start no lighter than **step 250** (`#86b6ef`,
2.06:1); on dark, go no darker than **step 600** (`#184f95`, 2.15:1).

## Diverging pair

**blue <-> red** - warm/cool poles that read as opposite. Neutral midpoint is gray
(light `#f0efec`, dark `#383835`). Equal step count per arm. (blue<->aqua was
rejected - both cool, the midpoint doesn't read as "nothing".)

## Status palette (fixed - never themed)

| role | hex | light-surface contrast | dark-surface contrast |
|---|---|---|---|
| good | `#0ca30c` | 3.27 | 5.19 |
| warning | `#fab219` | 1.79 | 9.49 |
| serious | `#ec835a` | 2.57 | 6.60 |
| critical | `#d03b3b` | 4.68 | 3.62 |

Dark: same four steps - all clear 3:1 on the dark surface (`#1a1a19`) and remain
distinct from the dark categorical slots. On the light surface, warning and
serious are sub-3:1 by design; the **icon + label** pairing is the mitigation, so
a status color never carries meaning alone. These steps are deliberately distinct
from the categorical slots so a status color never impersonates a series -
distinct enough that nothing collides at a glance, not enough for hue to
carry the distinction unaided: measured by the series floor's own bar
(unsimulated Delta E >= 15), around nine categorical-vs-status pairs per mode sit
below 15 - in light mode red vs critical and yellow vs warning both measure
4.8, slot-2 orange sits 5.8 from status-serious, and the light success text
green `#006300` sits 10.1 from the series green; green vs status-good (9.7)
holds in both modes, since both hexes are mode-invariant. The rule is general: any series color beside a
same-hue-family status or delta cue leans on the icon + label pairing and on
placement; never on hue alone.

## Texture fill (the accessibility channel)

One hand-drawn **"Lines"** fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror only**. Inked
tone-on-tone (a darker step of the fill's own ramp). On value scales it is
*ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging sign).
Triggered by the accessibility setting, print, or `forced-colors` - never
decorative, never on by default.

## Surfaces (for the validator)

- Light chart surface: `#fcfcfb`
- Dark chart surface: `#1a1a19`

These are the validator's built-in defaults. **When you swap in your own
palette, re-run against your own surfaces:**
`--surface <your-light> --mode light` and `--surface <your-dark> --mode dark` -
contrast and band results are only meaningful against the surface the chart
actually renders on.

## Chart chrome & ink

| Role | Light | Dark |
|---|---|---|
| Chart surface | `#fcfcfb` | `#1a1a19` |
| Page plane | `#f9f9f7` | `#0d0d0d` |
| Primary ink | `#0b0b0b` | `#f0efec` |
| Secondary ink | `#52514e` | `#c3c2b7` |
| Muted (axis/labels) | `#898781` | `#898781` |
| Label inside a categorical or status fill | `#ffffff`, except `#0b0b0b` on yellow and warning | `#ffffff`, except `#0b0b0b` on warning |
| Gridline (hairline) | `#e1e0d9` | `#2c2c2a` |
| Baseline / axis | `#c3c2b7` | `#383835` |
| Delta up good (success text) | `#006300` | `#0ca30c` |
| Border (hairline ring) | `rgba(11,11,11,0.10)` | `rgba(255,255,255,0.10)` |

## Filter controls

Filters are standard UI, not chart components - the chart layer only adds the
composition rules in `interaction.md`. A date-range control is a list of preset
rows (today, last 7/30/90 days, month-to-date) with selection marked by a 16px
bold check, hover as a ghost wash, and custom range behind a hairline in the
footer. Dimension filters are a standard combobox.

## Typeface & figures

Everything - including the hero figure - stays in the system sans: `system-ui,
-apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif`. No display or serif face anywhere. Large
standalone numbers (hero figure, stat-tile values) use the default proportional
figures; reserve `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns that must align
vertically (table rows, axis ticks). Substitute your brand's UI sans here.

placement; never on hue alone.

One hand-drawn **"Lines"** fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror only**. Inked
tone-on-tone (a darker step of the fill's own ramp). On value scales it is
*ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging sign).
Triggered by the accessibility setting, print, or `forced-colors` - never
decorative, never on by default.

## Surfaces (for the validator)

- Light chart surface: `#fcfcfb`
- Dark chart surface: `#1a1a19`

palette, re-run against your own surfaces:**

contrast and band results are only meaningful against the surface the chart
actually renders on.

| Role | Light | Dark |
|---|---|---|

| Page plane | `#f9f9f7` | `#0d0d0d` |
| Primary ink | `#0b0b0b` | `#f0efec` |
| Secondary ink | `#52514e` | `#c3c2b7` |
| Muted (axis/labels) | `#898781` | `#898781` |
| Label inside a categorical or status fill | `#ffffff`, except `#0b0b0b` on yellow and warning | `#ffffff`, except `#0b0b0b` on warning |
| Gridline (hairline) | `#e1e0d9` | `#2c2c2a` |
| Baseline / axis | `#c3c2b7` | `#383835` |
| Delta up good (success text) | `#006300` | `#0ca30c` |
| Border (hairline ring) | `rgba(11,11,11,0.10)` | `rgba(255,255,255,0.10)` |

## Filter controls

Filters are standard UI, not chart components - the chart layer only adds the
composition rules in `interaction.md`. A date-range control is a list of preset
rows (today, last 7/30/90 days, month-to-date) with selection marked by a 16px
bold check, hover as a ghost wash, and custom range behind a hairline in the
footer. Dimension filters are a standard combobox.

## Typeface & figures

Everything - including the hero figure - stays in the system sans: `system-ui,
-apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif`. No display or serif face anywhere. Large
standalone numbers (hero figure, stat-tile values) use the default proportional
figures; reserve `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns that must align
vertically (table rows, axis ticks). Substitute your brand's UI sans here.
