======
# Marks & anatomy

The quiet, considered look is a few fixed specs plus two pieces of negative space.
The data is the only thing allowed to be loud.

## Mark specs (fixed across every chart)

| Mark | Spec |
|---|---|
| Bar / column | **<= 24px thick** (cap it - never fill the slot; let the band's leftover be air); **4px rounded data-end, square at the baseline**; grows from a single baseline |
| Line | **2px**, round join/cap |
| Marker / end-dot | **>= 8px** (r >= 4), filled with the series color |
| Area fill | the series hue at **~10% opacity** (a wash, never a saturated block) |
| Gridlines / axes | one-step-off-surface gray, **hairline (1px), solid** (never dashed), recessive |

## The two spacers (white doing the separating)

- **Surface gap.** A **2px gap** in the surface color separates touching marks - every
  segment of a stacked bar, and every adjacent (touching) bar, the same width. Keep it
  one consistent width across a stack; neighbors one step apart read distinct because of
  the gap, not a stroke drawn around them.
- **Surface ring.** Dots and end-markers carry a **2px ring in the surface color**,
  so they stay legible where they cross a line or overlap each other. The ring is part
  of the mark's hover/hit target, not just spacing - see `interaction.md` (small dots
  are easy to under-size for hover).

Never draw a border around a mark to separate it. The gap and the ring are the
mechanism; a stroke adds data-weight ink that isn't data.

## Labels & legend

A **legend is always present for two or more series** - the dependable identity
channel; never make the reader rely on color-matching alone. Direct labels then ride
the marks to *supplement* it. **A single series needs no legend box**: there is only
one color, so the chart's title or subtitle already says what is plotted. A box with
one swatch restates the title and costs space.

- **Label selectively - never a number on every point.** A value beside every dot or
  segment is chaos and goes unread. Label the endpoint, the extreme, or the one series
  the story is about; let the axis, the legend, and the tooltip/table carry the rest.
  Direct labels work *because* they are sparing - flood the chart and they stop working.
- **Direct labels before gridlines; gridlines before a second axis.**
- **A label that won't fit doesn't get clipped - measure first.** Only place a label
  *inside* a bar or stacked segment when the rendered text fits with comfortable
  padding on both sides. If it doesn't fit: for a whole bar/column, move the label
  outside the bar end (or to the tooltip if there's no room outside either); for an
  *interior* stacked segment (which has no free end),
  skip the inline label and let the legend + tooltip carry it. Either way the value
  stays in the table view, so nothing is gated. Never use `overflow: hidden` on the
  segment to "solve" it - that crops the first/last characters and is worse than no
  label. Text never overflows or is clipped by its own mark.
- Bars -> value at the tip. Columns -> value on the cap. Lines -> value at the end.
- Y-axis ticks: round to clean numbers, in full under 10,000 (0 / 1,000 / 2,000) and
  compact on an axis that reaches it (0 / 10K / 20K), one style per axis; along a
  horizontal axis, in full under a million where the labels fit side by side. They
  carry the values you didn't directly label, so keep them unless every value is labeled.
- **Text never wears the data color.** Marks - bars, lines, dots, area fills - carry
  the series color; labels, values, legends, and axis text use **text tokens**
  (primary / secondary / muted). A light categorical hue (yellow, aqua) is illegible
  as text on the surface. Identity comes from the colored mark *beside* the text - a
  dot, a short line-key, a swatch - never from coloring the text itself. A label set
  *inside* a colored fill (a stacked segment, a map tile) is the one exception: white or
  near-black, the same two in both modes, by the fill's luminance. `palette.md` says which its
  categorical and status colors take.
- **When end-labels collide, don't stack them.** Direct end-labels work when series
  separate at the right edge. When lines converge, nudging labels apart vertically
  detaches them from their lines and reads as noise - instead use **leader lines**
  (a thin connector from label to line-end), facet into **small multiples**, or fall
  back to the legend + tooltip. Past ~4 converging series, small multiples is usually right.

## Figures - when the form is a number

- **Stat tile** contract: `label` (sentence case, no trailing colon) · `value` (Sans
  semibold, auto-compact: 1,284 / 12.9K / $4.2M) · `delta` (optional; signed,
  vs a named period; color = direction × whether up is good) · `trend` (optional;
  12-point sparkline in the de-emphasis hue, current period in the accent).
- **Meter:** the fill carries severity (accent -> warning -> danger); the unfilled
  track is a **lighter step of the same ramp** (blue-on-blue, etc.) so state reads
  across the whole bar.
- **Segmented bar - one whole, split into parts.** A figure, thin or tall, with no baseline, so
  no end is square. Widths proportional to the values; a part at zero draws nothing.
  **Thin:** 8px, or 4px in dense rows; fully rounded ends; no text. **Tall:** 28px and never
  more; each part its own block, 4px corners, its share (46%) or rounded amount (413M)
  printed inside at the leading edge, in white or near-black (*Labels & legend* says which).
  A block too narrow for its label prints none: that value stays in the table view.
  Hover, keyboard focus, and the bar's accessible name give every part's name, amount, and
  share. The legend lists the names in block order and repeats no numbers. The tall bar is
  exempt from four chart rules: the 24px bar cap, the ban on large saturated blocks, the ban
  on a number on every point, and direct name labels (its legend names the parts). It keeps
  its legend and its table view.
- **Hero figure.** The single number a dashboard leads with, >=48px, in the same
  sans as everything else (never a display or serif face - it reads as off-brand
  decoration). Exactly one per view.
- **Proportional figures for big numbers; tabular only in columns.** A large
  standalone value (hero figure, stat-tile value) uses the font's default
  proportional figures - `tabular-nums` gives every digit the width of a `0`, so a
  number like `121` looks loose at display sizes. Reserve
  `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns of numbers that must align
  vertically (table rows, axis ticks).

## Texture - the backup channel (opt-in)

Where hue fails - full-severity CVD, grayscale print, `forced-colors` - texture
carries identity. One directional hand-drawn fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror
only** (never horizontal/vertical - those read as gridlines/bars). Inked tone-on-tone
(a step from the fill's own ramp), equal loudness across slots. On value scales the
texture is *ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging
sign) so it never misstates the value. Triggered by an accessibility setting, print,
or `forced-colors` - never on by default. (See `palette.md`.)

## Task 2.2: Frontend Task Board

| Deliverable | Where |
|---|---|
| React component (TypeScript, hooks) | [`web/src/features/board/TaskBoard.tsx`](../../web/src/features/board/TaskBoard.tsx) and its children in the same folder |
| Tests | Unit tests for filters and drag-and-drop maths, a real-cache test of the optimistic move, and component tests for every state ([`web/src/**/*.test.ts(x)`](../../web/src/features/board/)) |

Run `npm run dev`, then open http://localhost:5173. Pick a project and a "view as" user in the header.

### State management and component architecture

**One container, presentational children.** `TaskBoard` owns the filters, two queries (`Board`: columns with their first page; `BoardSummary`: counts and chart data) and the move action. `FilterBar`, `SummaryPanel`, `Board`, `BoardColumn` and `TaskCard` receive props and raise callbacks. Their only state is local UI state, such as an open dropdown, a dragged card or a "load more" spinner.

**Each kind of state has one home, and there's no global store:**

- **Server data** lives in Apollo's normalised cache: each task and column is stored once by id. A column's pages, whether from the board query or that column's "load more" (`taskStatus(id)`), merge into one list.
- **Project and filters** live in the URL, read through `useSyncExternalStore`. Links are shareable, and Back undoes a filter.
- **The session** ("view as") is React context. Switching user resets the Apollo cache, so one user's data never shows for another.

**Moves never refetch the board.** A drop updates the card optimistically and edits only the two affected cached lists. It adds the card only to filtered views that contained it, then refetches just the small summary. If the server refuses, Apollo discards the optimistic layer and the card snaps back.

**Every state is handled:**

- **First load:** a skeleton.
- **Filter changes:** the previous board stays on screen, dimmed.
- **Errors:** a retryable error state.
- **Empty:** "no tasks yet" is told apart from "no matches", which offers Clear filters.
- **Viewers:** a read-only board.

**Accessibility and performance:**

- **Accessibility:** drag-and-drop works from the keyboard, with screen-reader announcements. The chart has a table equivalent, and overdue is never shown by colour alone.
- **Colours:** checked with a palette validator in light and dark mode.
- **Performance:** the chart is code-split, which cuts initial JavaScript from 892 kB to 488 kB.

# Part 2: Full-Stack Implementation

## Task 2.1: Backend GraphQL API

| Deliverable                       | Where                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| GraphQL schema (type definitions) | [`api/src/graphql/schema.graphql`](../../api/src/graphql/schema.graphql)                                                                                                                                                  |
| Resolver implementation           | [`api/src/graphql/resolvers.ts`](../../api/src/graphql/resolvers.ts), with SQL in [`api/src/repositories/tasks.ts`](../../api/src/repositories/tasks.ts) and batching in [`loaders.ts`](../../api/src/graphql/loaders.ts) |
| Tests                             | [`api/test/graphql.test.ts`](../../api/test/graphql.test.ts) (every result checked against SQL ground truth) and [`graphql-contract.test.ts`](../../api/test/graphql-contract.test.ts)                                    |

Run it with `npm run setup` then `npm run dev`. GraphiQL is at http://localhost:4000/graphql, and http://localhost:4000/dev/users gives a token for every seeded user.

### Design decisions

**The contract comes first.** The SDL is a strict subset of the Part 1 design (a test enforces it), and GraphQL Code Generator types every resolver against it, so drift fails the build.

**Authorization is enforced by Postgres, not by memory.** Each GraphQL operation runs in one transaction as `app_user`, with the caller's id set, so row-level security filters every query. Resolvers get only that transaction; no unscoped database handle exists. Other tenants' ids return `null` or `NOT_FOUND`, never "forbidden", and database messages are masked.

**The query count is constant.** Per-request DataLoaders batch every relation. All board columns page in one `LATERAL` query, and `identifier` and `isOverdue` are computed in SQL. A test proves a board load issues the same number of queries for 5 or 50 cards per column. The summary is one `GROUPING SETS` pass.

**Pagination is keyset-based.** Cursors encode `(sort value, id)`, never timestamps, so JavaScript's millisecond precision can't skip rows. Sorts use index-friendly keys, with undated tasks last. `first` is capped at 100 and query depth at 10.

**`moveTask` is safe under concurrency.** The server computes a fractional rank between the neighbours while holding a per-column advisory lock, so concurrent drops can't produce the same key. A failed mutation rolls back entirely.

**Trade-off:** a transaction holds its connection for the whole operation, so resolvers may only wait on the database. The summary still scans the project on every request, which Part 3 addresses.

The board needs to load more cards for **one** column; re-running the board query with an `after` cursor would apply one column's cursor to every column. With the column addressable by id, Apollo merges its next page into the same cached list (tested in `api/test/graphql.test.ts`).

**One container, presentational children.** `TaskBoard` owns the filters, two queries (`Board`: columns with their first page; `BoardSummary`: counts and chart data) and the move action. `FilterBar`, `SummaryPanel`, `Board`, `BoardColumn` and `TaskCard` receive props and raise callbacks. Their only state is local UI state, such as an open dropdown, a dragged card or a "load more" spinner.

  FilterBar, SummaryPanel, Board, BoardColumn, TaskCard are presentational.

  (relayStylePagination merges a column's "load more" into the same list),
  URL (useSyncExternalStore) for project + filters, React context for the
  "view as" session (switch resets the cache), local useState for UI only.
- Drag-and-drop (dnd-kit, keyboard + pointer, identifier-based screen
  reader announcements): optimistic moveTask, cache edited only for the two
  columns and only in filtered views that contained the card; refetches the
  summary only; automatic rollback on error, reload on CONFLICT.
- States: skeleton, dimmed previous board while filters change, retryable
  error, "no tasks yet" vs "no matches" (Clear filters), viewer read-only.
- Priority chart (Recharts) per the dataviz method: single series, one
  validated hue (light + dark), value at bar tips, hover tooltip, sr-only
  table; overdue uses the reserved critical color with icon + text.
- Chart code-split: initial JS 892 kB -> 488 kB.
- API: Query.taskStatus(id) (design SDL + API + test) so one column can
  page without re-running every column.
- API tests capped at 3 workers: a PGlite worker ran out of memory with
  unbounded parallelism next to running dev servers.

states); API 55. Verified in headless Chrome, light + dark (screenshots in

Task 2.2 is built and committed (`c6134cf`), which completes Part 2. I ran it against the real API with the 2,500-task project and screenshotted it in light and dark mode (both in `docs/part2/images/`). One gap: **I haven't done a real mouse or keyboard drag in a browser.**

## What it does
- **Kanban board:** columns per status, with true per-column counts. Each column loads 25 cards and has its own "Load more".
- **Drag and drop:** works with mouse and keyboard, and screen readers hear "Picked up WEB-42…". The card moves instantly; only the summary is refetched, the board isn't reloaded; it snaps back if the server refuses.
- **Filters:** assignee, priority, label, due-date range and overdue only. They're stored in the URL, so a filtered board is a shareable link and Back undoes a change.
- **Summary:** total, overdue, completed and unassigned tiles, plus a "tasks by priority" bar chart.
- **States:** a loading skeleton; the previous board shown dimmed while filters change; a retryable error; "no tasks yet" told apart from "no matches" (with Clear filters); and a read-only badge for viewers.
- **"View as" switcher** in the header. Switching user clears Apollo's cache, so one user's data never shows for another.

The 294-word explanation of state management and component architecture is in `docs/part2/README.md`.

## Checks
- **Tests:** web 14 and API 55, all passing. They cover the filter logic, the drag-and-drop position maths, the instant move against a real Apollo cache, and every board state.
- **Chart:** follows the dataviz method, with the colours run through its validator for light and dark mode. Overdue is never shown by colour alone, and the chart has a table for screen readers.

## Problems I hit and fixed
- **The frontend install silently didn't happen**, because my `| tail -1` hid the output. I caught it when a folder was missing and reran it.
- **The screenshots showed a layout gap** above the board and missing thousands separators, both fixed.
- **The bundle was 892 kB.** Loading the chart separately cut what the board needs at startup to 488 kB.
- **The API test suite crashed with out-of-memory.** Each test file starts its own WebAssembly Postgres, and the dev servers and Chrome were also running. I capped it at 3 test files at a time.

## Decisions to flag
1. **New API field `Query.taskStatus(id)`,** added to both the design and the API with a test. Without it, "load more" for one column would have applied that column's cursor to every column. It's recorded in the schema changelog.
2. **The default project is MOB**, because it's first alphabetically. Pick **WEB · Website Relaunch** to see the 2,500-task board.
3. **Two rough edges remain:**
   - Bars with zero tasks show no "0" label (the screen-reader table has the zeros).
   - A card dragged into another column lands *above* the card it's dropped on; the other cards don't shift aside during the drag.

## Try it
```
npm run dev      # then open http://localhost:5173
```
`db:serve` (DBeaver) and `npm run dev` can't run at the same time.

**Next:** Part 3, the RFC on the slow 2,000-task board. The measurements we already have can support it: the 76 ms board load, the constant query count, the scan cost of the summary, and the 892 → 488 kB bundle. Shall I start?

Starting Part 3. The RFC will be much stronger if its "problem" and "evidence" sections use **measured numbers** rather than estimates. We have a prototype of the proposed design (Part 2), so I can compare it directly with the "fetch everything" approach the scenario describes, on the same data.

I'll measure, on a 2,500-task project and on a 20,000-task project (10× the scenario):
- **Fetch everything:** payload size and time for all cards.
- **Board query:** a first page of each column plus the summary.
- **Summary alone:** time.
- **SQL statements** per board load.

These are PGlite numbers, so I'll present them as relative comparisons, never as production latencies.

lines: -// Throw-away probe (deleted after running): evidence for the Part 3 RFC.
-// Compares "fetch every card" (the scenario's current behaviour) with the Part 2 design
-// (first page per column + one-pass summary), on 2,500 and 20,000-task projects.
-// PGlite on a dev laptop: use the numbers as RATIOS, not production latencies.
-const CARD = `id identifier title priority dueDate isOverdue status { id } assignee { id displayName } labels { id name color }`;
-const BOARD = `query ($p: ID!) { project(id: $p) { statuses { id name tasks(first: 25) {
-  edges { cursor node { ${CARD} } } pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor } } }
-  taskSummary { total overdue byStatus { count status { id } } byPriority { priority count } byAssignee { count assignee { id } } } } }`;
-const PAGE = `query ($p: ID!, $after: String) { project(id: $p) { tasks(first: 100, after: $after) {
-const SUMMARY = `query ($p: ID!) { project(id: $p) { taskSummary { total overdue byPriority { priority count } } } }`;
-  const t = await createTestApp({ largeProjectTasks: size });
-  console.log(`\n=== project with ${size.toLocaleString()} tasks (seeded in ${((Date.now() - started) / 1000).toFixed(0)} s)`);
-  // Warm-up (plan caches, wasm JIT), then median of 5 runs.
-  // 1) New design: board = first 25 per column + summary, one request.
-    const response = await t.gql('carol', BOARD, { p: web });
-  const boardMs = await median(() => t.gql('carol', BOARD, { p: web }));
-  console.log(`board (25/column + summary): ${kb(boardBytes)} JSON, ${boardQueries} SQL statements, median ${boardMs.toFixed(0)} ms`);
-  // 2) "Fetch everything": every card with the same fields (paged at the API's 100 cap).
-    const response: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof t.gql<{ project: { tasks: { edges: unknown[]; pageInfo: { hasNextPage: boolean; endCursor: string | null } } } }>>> =
-      await t.gql('carol', PAGE, { p: web, after });
-  console.log(`all cards: ${cards.toLocaleString()} cards, ${kb(allBytes)} JSON, ${pages} requests, total ${allMs.toFixed(0)} ms`);
-  // 3) The summary alone — the part whose cost still grows with project size.
-  const summaryMs = await median(() => t.gql('carol', SUMMARY, { p: web }));
-  // 4) What N+1 resolvers would cost for "fetch everything" (arithmetic, not measured):
-  console.log(`naive N+1 for all cards: 1 + ${cards} x 3 (assignee, labels, status) = ${(1 + cards * 3).toLocaleString()} SQL statements`);

# RFC: A Fast Task Board for Large Projects

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | Draft, for review |
| **Author** | Mayank (drafted with Claude Code) |
| **Reviewers** | Board team engineers, product manager |
| **Decision needed** | Approve option B and the rollout plan; answer the open questions in §9 |
| **Evidence** | A working prototype on the real schema (Part 2) and measurements on 2,500- and 20,000-task projects |

## 1. Summary

The task board takes **6–8 seconds** to load for projects with 2,000+ tasks, and every filter change or drag-and-drop repeats that wait. The cause is architectural: the board downloads **every task** of the project, renders all of them, and re-downloads everything after any change.

We propose loading the board **one page per column** (about 25 cards), with filters and counts computed on the server, and making a drag-and-drop update **only the two affected columns** in the client's cache. A prototype on our schema loads a 20,000-task board with the same 57 KB, 11 SQL statements and about 50 ms of server time as a 2,500-task board. Fetching everything costs **7.7 MB and 9.7 s** at 20,000 tasks.

## 2. Problem

**What users see:** 6–8 s to open a large board, the same delay on every filter change, and a full reload after every drag. The board is "unusable" at the size of our most active projects.

**Where the time goes.** We reproduced the "fetch everything" pattern on our schema and data, with the same card fields through the same GraphQL API:

| Cost driver | 2,500 tasks | 20,000 tasks | Grows with |
|---|---|---|---|
| Response payload (JSON) | 958 KB | 7.7 MB | Every task |
| Server time, even with batched lookups | 428 ms | 9.7 s | Every task |
| SQL statements if lookups aren't batched (assignee, labels and status per card) | 7,501 | 60,001 | Every task × 3 |
| DOM nodes to render, and drag targets to register | ~2,500 cards | ~20,000 cards | Every task |
| Work repeated on each filter change or move | All of the above | All of the above | Every interaction |

These measurements come from an embedded Postgres on a laptop. The **ratios** are what matter, not the absolute milliseconds. The client-side render cost wasn't measured here; Phase 0 instruments it.

**Who is affected:** the platform has 500+ organizations. We expect large projects to be concentrated in our biggest and most engaged customers. Phase 0 will confirm the share of projects, and of daily board views, above 2,000 tasks.

**Why it matters:** the board is the product's main screen. A screen that gets slower the more a team uses it punishes our best customers first, so this is a retention risk before it is a performance problem.

## 3. Goals and non-goals

**Goals:**
- Board load, filtering and drag-and-drop feel instant at 2,000 tasks.
- They stay that way at 20,000 tasks (10× headroom).
- Existing clients and integrations keep working throughout.

**Non-goals for this RFC:**
- Real-time updates pushed from other users.
- Offline mode.
- Full-text search.
- Changing the board's visual design.

## 4. Performance targets

Measured in production with real-user monitoring (RUM), for projects with 2,000–20,000 tasks.

| Metric | Today | Target p75 | Target p95 | Prototype (laptop) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Board load: first cards visible (LCP) | 6–8 s | ≤ 1.0 s | ≤ 2.0 s | — |
| Board API response, server side | ~0.4–9.7 s | ≤ 150 ms | ≤ 300 ms | 22 ms (2.5k) / 49 ms (20k) |
| Payload per board load | 1–8 MB, grows with the project | ≤ 80 KB, constant | ≤ 120 KB | 57 KB at both sizes |
| SQL statements per board load | Up to 60,000 | ≤ 12, constant | ≤ 12 | 11 at both sizes |
| Filter change → updated board | 6–8 s (full reload) | ≤ 300 ms | ≤ 600 ms | — |
| Drag-and-drop response (INP) | Full reload | ≤ 100 ms | ≤ 200 ms | Instant (optimistic) |
| Move confirmed by the server | — | ≤ 150 ms | ≤ 300 ms | 52 ms |
| Board refetches per move | 1 (everything) | 0 (summary only) | 0 | 0 |
| Initial JavaScript (gzipped) | — | ≤ 160 KB | — | 148 KB |
| Move error rate (excluding stale-board conflicts) | — | < 0.1% | — | — |

"Good" means the bottom four rows hold at **20,000 tasks** in a load test (Phase 3), not just at 2,000.

## 5. Options considered

### A. Optimise the client, keep fetching everything

Virtualise the columns, memoise cards, filter client-side, and make moves optimistic.

- **For:** no API change; about 2 weeks.
- **Against:** it fixes rendering but not data volume. Every load still transfers 1–8 MB and costs the server 0.4–9.7 s, filtering client-side means holding every task in browser memory, and the cost keeps growing with the project.

### B. A server-driven board (recommended)

Each column is a cursor-paginated list (25 cards, then "load more"), and filters run in SQL. One aggregate query returns the column counts and the chart data. A move is a mutation that returns only the moved card; the client edits its cached copy of the two columns and refetches only the summary.

- **For:** load cost depends on the number of columns, not the number of tasks (57 KB and 11 statements at both sizes). Filters reuse the same indexed queries. A move transfers one card.
- **Against:** a larger API; more complex cache logic on the client; counts come from a separate query; finding a card beyond the loaded pages needs server-side search.

### C. A local-first sync engine (Linear-style)

Sync the whole project into an in-browser database and push changes over websockets; every read is then local.

- **For:** everything is instant; offline support and real-time collaboration come with it.
- **Against:** quarters of work, not weeks:
  - the first sync still downloads everything (7.7 MB at 20,000 tasks);
  - tenancy and permissions must be enforced in the sync protocol;
  - it needs conflict resolution;
  - memory pressure on low-end devices.

  The right long-term direction *if* real-time collaboration becomes a product goal; too large for the current pain.

### Comparison

| | A: client-only | **B: server-driven** | C: local-first |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixes first load at 2k / 20k tasks | Partly / no | **Yes / yes** | First sync slow / no |
| Fixes filters and moves | Yes | **Yes** | Yes |
| Server and database load | Unchanged | **Constant per view** | Shifted to sync |
| Effort | ~2 weeks | **~6 weeks + rollout** | Quarters |
| Risk | Low | **Medium** | High |

## 6. Recommendation

**Option B.** We take A's virtualisation only if Phase 0 data shows long, fully loaded columns still dropping frames; paging already keeps the number of rendered cards small. C stays on the roadmap as the path to real-time collaboration.

**B is already proven on our schema.** The Part 2 prototype implements it end to end:
- Pagination per column uses keyset cursors, and all columns load in one SQL round trip (`LATERAL`).
- Counts and the chart come from a single `GROUPING SETS` pass.
- Lookups are batched per request (DataLoader), and a test proves the SQL statement count stays constant as pages grow.
- `moveTask` computes the card's new position on the server between the given neighbours, under a per-column lock so concurrent drops can't collide.
- On the client, moves are optimistic and edit only the two affected columns; the chart is code-split.

## 7. Implementation plan

Two engineers, about 6 weeks plus the rollout.

| Phase | Weeks | Work | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0. Measure** | 1 | Real-user monitoring of board load, interaction latency, payload and SQL count, bucketed by project size; server tracing; the `board_v2` feature flag | Baselines agreed; affected-project share known |
| **1. API** | 2–3 | Per-column connection, `taskStatus(id)` and server-side filters; `taskSummary`; DataLoaders; `moveTask` with server-computed position; board index built with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`; backfill position keys from today's ordering in batches (expand/contract) | Contract tests green; query-count test; load test at 20,000 tasks meets the API targets |
| **2. Client** | 3–5 | `board_v2` behind the flag: column paging with infinite scroll, filters in the URL, optimistic moves, summary-only refetch, loading, error and empty states, code-split chart | Component tests; LCP and INP targets met on staging data |
| **3. Harden** | 6 | Load test (20,000 tasks, 50 concurrent boards); handling for stale boards (`CONFLICT`); accessibility review; decision on virtualisation | All §4 targets met in staging |
| **4. Roll out** | 7–9 | See §8 | 100% of organizations; old path deprecated |

The API changes are **additive**: the existing "all tasks" query keeps working until no client uses it.

## 8. Rollout strategy

1. **Ship the API first, unused:** the new fields go live behind no flag, because they're additive. A shadow job compares the new summary counts with the old full-load counts for a sample of projects, which catches filter or permission bugs before any user sees them.
2. **Turn the new board on in stages,** per organization, through the `board_v2` flag:

   | Stage | Organizations | Duration |
   |---|---|---|
   | Internal | Our own | 3 days |
   | Opt-in beta | Customers with the largest projects (~5%) | 1 week |
   | Wider | 25% → 50% | 3 days each |
   | All | 100% | — |

3. **Gate every stage** on four checks: p95 board load ≤ 2 s; move error rate < 0.1%; no rise in board-related support tickets; count parity above 99.9%.
4. **Keep a kill switch:** turning the flag off restores the old board instantly. The database changes are expand-only, so a rollback never needs a migration.
5. **Communicate:** release notes from the PM, and a "new board" badge with a temporary "switch back" link during the beta. Support gets a macro for the two visible behaviour changes: counts come from the summary, and cards beyond the first page load on scroll.
6. **Clean up:** two releases after 100%, mark the "all tasks" query `@deprecated`, watch its usage drop to zero, then remove it together with the old board code.

## 9. Risks and open questions

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Counts briefly disagree with the loaded cards after a move | Counts always come from the summary, which is refetched after every move |
| Another user's change isn't visible until a refresh (no real-time updates) | Refresh when the window regains focus; `CONFLICT` reloads the affected column. Real-time updates are a separate RFC |
| The summary is the one query whose cost grows with the project (10 → 41 ms from 2,500 to 20,000 tasks) | Cache it per project and filter for a few seconds. Above ~100,000 tasks, maintain per-status counter rows instead |
| Position keys grow after many drops into the same gap | Length limit in the database; a periodic rebalance job per column |
| Old mobile clients depend on the "all tasks" query | Kept and deprecated, removed only when usage reaches zero |

**Open questions for product:**
- Is "updates on refresh" acceptable for v2, or is real-time a launch requirement?
- Must column counts be exact at very large sizes, or is "1,000+" acceptable?
- Should each column remember its own sort (priority, due date) or always use manual order?
- What is the mobile app's migration timeline?

Each column is a cursor-paginated list (25 cards, then "load more"), and filters run in SQL. One aggregate query returns the column counts and the chart data. A move is a mutation that returns only the moved card; the client edits its cached copy of the two columns and refetches only the summary.

- **For:** load cost depends on the number of columns, not the number of tasks (57 KB and 11 statements at both sizes). Filters reuse the same indexed queries. A move transfers one card.
- **Against:** a larger API; more complex cache logic on the client; counts come from a separate query; finding a card beyond the loaded pages needs server-side search.

### C. A local-first sync engine (Linear-style)

Sync the whole project into an in-browser database and push changes over websockets; every read is then local.

- **For:** everything is instant; offline support and real-time collaboration come with it.
- **Against:** quarters of work, not weeks:
  - the first sync still downloads everything (7.7 MB at 20,000 tasks);
  - tenancy and permissions must be enforced in the sync protocol;
  - it needs conflict resolution;
  - memory pressure on low-end devices.

  The right long-term direction *if* real-time collaboration becomes a product goal; too large for the current pain.

### Comparison

| | A: client-only | **B: server-driven** | C: local-first |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixes first load at 2k / 20k tasks | Partly / no | **Yes / yes** | First sync slow / no |
| Fixes filters and moves | Yes | **Yes** | Yes |
| Server and database load | Unchanged | **Constant per view** | Shifted to sync |
| Effort | ~2 weeks | **~6 weeks + rollout** | Quarters |
| Risk | Low | **Medium** | High |

## 6. Recommendation

**Option B.** We take A's virtualisation only if Phase 0 data shows long, fully loaded columns still dropping frames; paging already keeps the number of rendered cards small. C stays on the roadmap as the path to real-time collaboration.

**B is already proven on our schema.** The Part 2 prototype implements it end to end:
- Pagination per column uses keyset cursors, and all columns load in one SQL round trip (`LATERAL`).
- Counts and the chart come from a single `GROUPING SETS` pass.
- Lookups are batched per request (DataLoader), and a test proves the SQL statement count stays constant as pages grow.
- `moveTask` computes the card's new position on the server between the given neighbours, under a per-column lock so concurrent drops can't collide.
- On the client, moves are optimistic and edit only the two affected columns; the chart is code-split.

## 7. Implementation plan

Two engineers, about 6 weeks plus the rollout.

| Phase | Weeks | Work | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0. Measure** | 1 | Real-user monitoring of board load, interaction latency, payload and SQL count, bucketed by project size; server tracing; the `board_v2` feature flag | Baselines agreed; affected-project share known |
| **1. API** | 2–3 | Per-column connection, `taskStatus(id)` and server-side filters; `taskSummary`; DataLoaders; `moveTask` with server-computed position; board index built with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`; backfill position keys from today's ordering in batches (expand/contract) | Contract tests green; query-count test; load test at 20,000 tasks meets the API targets |
| **2. Client** | 3–5 | `board_v2` behind the flag: column paging with infinite scroll, filters in the URL, optimistic moves, summary-only refetch, loading, error and empty states, code-split chart | Component tests; LCP and INP targets met on staging data |
| **3. Harden** | 6 | Load test (20,000 tasks, 50 concurrent boards); handling for stale boards (`CONFLICT`); accessibility review; decision on virtualisation | All §4 targets met in staging |
| **4. Roll out** | 7–9 | See §8 | 100% of organizations; old path deprecated |

The API changes are **additive**: the existing "all tasks" query keeps working until no client uses it.

## 8. Rollout strategy

1. **Ship the API first, unused:** the new fields go live behind no flag, because they're additive. A shadow job compares the new summary counts with the old full-load counts for a sample of projects, which catches filter or permission bugs before any user sees them.
2. **Turn the new board on in stages,** per organization, through the `board_v2` flag:

   | Stage | Organizations | Duration |
   |---|---|---|
   | Internal | Our own | 3 days |
   | Opt-in beta | Customers with the largest projects (~5%) | 1 week |
   | Wider | 25% → 50% | 3 days each |
   | All | 100% | — |

3. **Gate every stage** on four checks: p95 board load ≤ 2 s; move error rate < 0.1%; no rise in board-related support tickets; count parity above 99.9%.
4. **Keep a kill switch:** turning the flag off restores the old board instantly. The database changes are expand-only, so a rollback never needs a migration.
5. **Communicate:** release notes from the PM, and a "new board" badge with a temporary "switch back" link during the beta. Support gets a macro for the two visible behaviour changes: counts come from the summary, and cards beyond the first page load on scroll.
6. **Clean up:** two releases after 100%, mark the "all tasks" query `@deprecated`, watch its usage drop to zero, then remove it together with the old board code.

## 9. Risks and open questions

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Counts briefly disagree with the loaded cards after a move | Counts always come from the summary, which is refetched after every move |
| Another user's change isn't visible until a refresh (no real-time updates) | Refresh when the window regains focus; `CONFLICT` reloads the affected column. Real-time updates are a separate RFC |
| The summary is the one query whose cost grows with the project (10 → 41 ms from 2,500 to 20,000 tasks) | Cache it per project and filter for a few seconds. Above ~100,000 tasks, maintain per-status counter rows instead |
| Position keys grow after many drops into the same gap | Length limit in the database; a periodic rebalance job per column |
| Old mobile clients depend on the "all tasks" query | Kept and deprecated, removed only when usage reaches zero |

**Open questions for product:**
- Is "updates on refresh" acceptable for v2, or is real-time a launch requirement?
- Must column counts be exact at very large sizes, or is "1,000+" acceptable?
- Should each column remember its own sort (priority, due date) or always use manual order?
- What is the mobile app's migration timeline?

content.text:
Part 3 is done and committed as `dde45cd`, which completes all three parts. One deliverable remains: the AI transcript.

## The RFC
[docs/part3/rfc-fast-task-board.md](docs/part3/rfc-fast-task-board.md) is about 1,770 words, written for the engineering team and the PM, and covers every section the brief asks for:

| Required section | What it says |
|---|---|
| Problem, with metrics | Where the 6–8 s goes. Downloading every card costs 958 KB and 0.4 s at 2,500 tasks, and **7.7 MB and 9.7 s at 20,000**. Without batched lookups that's 60,001 SQL queries. |
| At least 2 options | **A:** speed up the browser only. **B:** a server-driven board, paged per column. **C:** a local-first sync engine (Linear-style). Each has its trade-offs and a comparison table. |
| Recommendation + plan | **B**, already proven by the Part 2 prototype. About six weeks in phases: measure, API, client, harden, roll out, each with exit criteria. |
| Performance targets | Production targets at p75 and p95, next to what the prototype achieved: board 57 KB, 11 queries and 22→49 ms, **flat from 2,500 to 20,000 tasks**. |
| Rollout | API changes are additive and ship first. A background job checks the new counts against the old ones. Then a per-organization feature flag in stages (internal → beta → 25% → 50% → 100%), each gated on metrics. Turning the flag off restores the old board instantly. |

It closes with risks and four open questions for product, such as whether real-time updates are needed for v2.

**How I kept it honest:**
- **Measured, not estimated:** I recreated the "download every card" approach on our own schema and data, and compared it with the Part 2 board.
- **Ratios, not latencies:** these are laptop timings on PGlite, so the RFC relies on the ratios between approaches.
- **Labelled baselines:** the reproduced "today" figures are marked as reproduced, so they can't be mistaken for production data.
- **Admitted gaps:** browser rendering cost wasn't measured; the RFC says so and makes measuring it Phase 0.

## What's left: the AI transcript
**Three logs make up the full record:**
- this session;
- your other session (`1921b779…`, Nov 6–16), where the Kysely/Drizzle/Sequelize comparisons and the date-parsing bug came from;
- the critique agent's own log.

**Suggested order:**
1. **Your prompting-strategy commentary** (the brief requires it). As with the analysis, I can draft it from what actually happened, with a provenance note, or you write it.
2. **Final README pass:** a full map of the deliverables, assumptions, and how to run everything.
3. **Export the transcripts last,** so they include everything:
   - run `/export` in **this** session and in your other session (Claude Code's built-in export);
   - I can also convert all three raw logs into readable Markdown under `docs/ai-transcript/`, unedited, with the raw files kept alongside;
   - **read it before publishing:** the logs contain local file paths and your git email.
4. **Push to GitHub.** `gh` isn't installed, so you'd create the repo and push yourself.

Shall I start with step 1 (the commentary draft) and step 2?

# CLAUDE.md

Working agreement for AI coding assistants on this repo. Humans: see README.md.

## Project

Take-home for Compliance Foundry: a multi-tenant project-management platform (organizations → projects → tasks). Deliverables are mapped in README.md, and stack rationale is in `docs/tech-stack-choice.md`.

## Rules

- **Comment all code.** Every new or modified block carries detailed comments covering what / why / how (plus which / where / when / who where relevant). Full rule: `.claude/memory/feedback_code_comments_mandatory.md`; team notes index: `.claude/memory/INDEX.md`.
- **Say "organization" everywhere.** Organization and workspace are the same tenant concept.
- **The SQL migrations in `api/db/migrations/` are the schema's source of truth.** They are forward-only. Never edit a committed migration; add a new one, then run `npm run db:codegen -w api` and commit the regenerated `api/src/db/types.ts`.
- **Kysely uses `CamelCasePlugin`.** TypeScript is `camelCase`, SQL is `snake_case`. Identifiers inside raw `sql` template text must be `snake_case`.
- **pg type parsers (`api/src/db/pool.ts`)**: `DATE` comes back as a `'YYYY-MM-DD'` string, and `int8` as a number (it throws if the value isn't a safe integer). Don't change these without updating codegen options and tests.
- **PGlite is one Postgres session.** Keep the pool and socket at one connection. Its timings are not production numbers.
- **Row-level security on PGlite.** The default user is a superuser, which bypasses RLS, so request transactions must `SET LOCAL ROLE`. Read custom settings with `nullif(current_setting('app.x', true), '')`: after first use, a setting reads as `''`, not NULL.
- **Workflow.** Go phase by phase as agreed with the user, wait for a go-ahead before starting a new phase, and run `npm run check` before calling anything done.

## Commands

| Command                      | What it does                                                                                           |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `npm run setup`              | Apply migrations and load demo data into the embedded dev database (`api/.pglite`)                     |
| `npm run dev`                | API on :4000 (GraphiQL at `/graphql`, dev tokens at `/dev/users`) + web board on http://localhost:5173 |
| `npm run check`              | Typecheck, lint, format check, verify generated types, run tests (also run in CI)                      |
| `npm test`                   | Tests only (each file boots a fresh in-memory PGlite)                                                  |
| `npm run db:serve`           | Serve the dev database on 127.0.0.1:54320 for DBeaver/psql until Ctrl+C (holds the data-folder lock)   |
| `npm run db:migrate -w api`  | Apply pending migrations                                                                               |
| `npm run db:reset -w api`    | Delete, re-migrate and re-seed the embedded dev database (refuses if `DATABASE_URL` is set)            |
| `npm run db:seed -w api`     | Load demo data into an empty database                                                                  |
| `npm run gql:codegen -w api` | Regenerate resolver types from `api/src/graphql/schema.graphql` (`-- --check` to verify)               |
| `npm run db:codegen -w api`  | Regenerate Kysely types from the migrations (`-- --verify` to check only)                              |

- [Compliance Foundry take-home](compliance-foundry-take-home.md) — assessment scope, deliverables, agreed phase-by-phase workflow
- [User: senior engineer](user-senior-engineer.md) — role and working-style preferences
- [Code comments rule](code-comments-rule.md) — detailed what/why/how comments on all code; source file in repo .claude/memory

# RFC: A Fast Task Board for Large Projects

|                     |                                                                                                     |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Status**          | Draft, for review                                                                                   |
| **Author**          | Mayank (drafted with Claude Code)                                                                   |
| **Reviewers**       | Board team engineers, product manager                                                               |
| **Decision needed** | Approve option B and the rollout plan; answer the open questions in §9                              |
| **Evidence**        | A working prototype on the real schema (Part 2) and measurements on 2,500- and 20,000-task projects |

## 1. Summary

The task board takes **6–8 seconds** to load for projects with 2,000+ tasks, and every filter change or drag-and-drop repeats that wait. The cause is architectural: the board downloads **every task** of the project, renders all of them, and re-downloads everything after any change.

We propose loading the board **one page per column** (about 25 cards), with filters and counts computed on the server, and making a drag-and-drop update **only the two affected columns** in the client's cache. A prototype on our schema loads a 20,000-task board with the same 57 KB, 11 SQL statements and about 50 ms of server time as a 2,500-task board. Fetching everything costs **7.7 MB and 9.7 s** at 20,000 tasks.

## 2. Problem

**What users see:** 6–8 s to open a large board, the same delay on every filter change, and a full reload after every drag. The board is "unusable" at the size of our most active projects.

**Where the time goes.** We reproduced the "fetch everything" pattern on our schema and data, with the same card fields through the same GraphQL API:

| Cost driver                                                                     | 2,500 tasks      | 20,000 tasks     | Grows with        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ----------------- |
| Response payload (JSON)                                                         | 958 KB           | 7.7 MB           | Every task        |
| Server time, even with batched lookups                                          | 428 ms           | 9.7 s            | Every task        |
| SQL statements if lookups aren't batched (assignee, labels and status per card) | 7,501            | 60,001           | Every task × 3    |
| DOM nodes to render, and drag targets to register                               | ~2,500 cards     | ~20,000 cards    | Every task        |
| Work repeated on each filter change or move                                     | All of the above | All of the above | Every interaction |

These measurements come from an embedded Postgres on a laptop. The **ratios** are what matter, not the absolute milliseconds. The client-side render cost wasn't measured here; Phase 0 instruments it.

**Who is affected:** the platform has 500+ organizations. We expect large projects to be concentrated in our biggest and most engaged customers. Phase 0 will confirm the share of projects, and of daily board views, above 2,000 tasks.

**Why it matters:** the board is the product's main screen. A screen that gets slower the more a team uses it punishes our best customers first, so this is a retention risk before it is a performance problem.

## 3. Goals and non-goals

**Goals:**

- Board load, filtering and drag-and-drop feel instant at 2,000 tasks.
- They stay that way at 20,000 tasks (10× headroom).
- Existing clients and integrations keep working throughout.

**Non-goals for this RFC:**

- Real-time updates pushed from other users.
- Offline mode.
- Full-text search.
- Changing the board's visual design.

## 4. Performance targets

Measured in production with real-user monitoring (RUM), for projects with 2,000–20,000 tasks.

| Metric                                            | Today                                       | Target p75        | Target p95 | Prototype (laptop)         |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ---------- | -------------------------- |
| Board load: first cards visible (LCP)             | 6–8 s                                       | ≤ 1.0 s           | ≤ 2.0 s    | —                          |
| Board API response, server side                   | 0.4–9.7 s (reproduced)                      | ≤ 150 ms          | ≤ 300 ms   | 22 ms (2.5k) / 49 ms (20k) |
| Payload per board load                            | 1–8 MB (reproduced), grows with the project | ≤ 80 KB, constant | ≤ 120 KB   | 57 KB at both sizes        |
| SQL statements per board load                     | Up to 60,000 (if unbatched)                 | ≤ 12, constant    | ≤ 12       | 11 at both sizes           |
| Filter change → updated board                     | 6–8 s (full reload)                         | ≤ 300 ms          | ≤ 600 ms   | —                          |
| Drag-and-drop response (INP)                      | Full reload                                 | ≤ 100 ms          | ≤ 200 ms   | Instant (optimistic)       |
| Move confirmed by the server                      | —                                           | ≤ 150 ms          | ≤ 300 ms   | 52 ms                      |
| Board refetches per move                          | 1 (everything)                              | 0 (summary only)  | 0          | 0                          |
| Initial JavaScript (gzipped)                      | —                                           | ≤ 160 KB          | —          | 148 KB                     |
| Move error rate (excluding stale-board conflicts) | —                                           | < 0.1%            | —          | —                          |

"Good" means the bottom four rows hold at **20,000 tasks** in a load test (Phase 3), not just at 2,000.

## 5. Options considered

### A. Optimise the client, keep fetching everything

Virtualise the columns, memoise cards, filter client-side, and make moves optimistic.

- **For:** no API change; about 2 weeks.
- **Against:** it fixes rendering but not data volume. Every load still transfers 1–8 MB and costs the server 0.4–9.7 s, filtering client-side means holding every task in browser memory, and the cost keeps growing with the project.

### B. A server-driven board (recommended)

Each column is a cursor-paginated list (25 cards, then "load more"), and filters run in SQL. One aggregate query returns the column counts and the chart data. A move is a mutation that returns only the moved card; the client edits its cached copy of the two columns and refetches only the summary.

- **For:** load cost depends on the number of columns, not the number of tasks (57 KB and 11 statements at both sizes). Filters reuse the same indexed queries. A move transfers one card.
- **Against:** a larger API; more complex cache logic on the client; counts come from a separate query; finding a card beyond the loaded pages needs server-side search.

### C. A local-first sync engine (Linear-style)

Sync the whole project into an in-browser database and push changes over websockets; every read is then local.

- **For:** everything is instant; offline support and real-time collaboration come with it.
- **Against:** quarters of work, not weeks:
  - the first sync still downloads everything (7.7 MB at 20,000 tasks);
  - tenancy and permissions must be enforced in the sync protocol;
  - it needs conflict resolution;
  - memory pressure on low-end devices.

  The right long-term direction _if_ real-time collaboration becomes a product goal; too large for the current pain.

### Comparison

|                                    | A: client-only | **B: server-driven**   | C: local-first       |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------- |
| Fixes first load at 2k / 20k tasks | Partly / no    | **Yes / yes**          | First sync slow / no |
| Fixes filters and moves            | Yes            | **Yes**                | Yes                  |
| Server and database load           | Unchanged      | **Constant per view**  | Shifted to sync      |
| Effort                             | ~2 weeks       | **~6 weeks + rollout** | Quarters             |
| Risk                               | Low            | **Medium**             | High                 |

## 6. Recommendation

**Option B.** We take A's virtualisation only if Phase 0 data shows long, fully loaded columns still dropping frames; paging already keeps the number of rendered cards small. C stays on the roadmap as the path to real-time collaboration.

**B is already proven on our schema.** The Part 2 prototype implements it end to end:

- Pagination per column uses keyset cursors, and all columns load in one SQL round trip (`LATERAL`).
- Counts and the chart come from a single `GROUPING SETS` pass.
- Lookups are batched per request (DataLoader), and a test proves the SQL statement count stays constant as pages grow.
- `moveTask` computes the card's new position on the server between the given neighbours, under a per-column lock so concurrent drops can't collide.
- On the client, moves are optimistic and edit only the two affected columns; the chart is code-split.

## 7. Implementation plan

Two engineers, about 6 weeks plus the rollout.

| Phase           | Weeks | Work                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Exit criteria                                                                           |
| --------------- | ----- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **0. Measure**  | 1     | Real-user monitoring of board load, interaction latency, payload and SQL count, bucketed by project size; server tracing; the `board_v2` feature flag                                                                                                                | Baselines agreed; affected-project share known                                          |
| **1. API**      | 2–3   | Per-column connection, `taskStatus(id)` and server-side filters; `taskSummary`; DataLoaders; `moveTask` with server-computed position; board index built with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`; backfill position keys from today's ordering in batches (expand/contract) | Contract tests green; query-count test; load test at 20,000 tasks meets the API targets |
| **2. Client**   | 3–5   | `board_v2` behind the flag: column paging with infinite scroll, filters in the URL, optimistic moves, summary-only refetch, loading, error and empty states, code-split chart                                                                                        | Component tests; LCP and INP targets met on staging data                                |
| **3. Harden**   | 6     | Load test (20,000 tasks, 50 concurrent boards); handling for stale boards (`CONFLICT`); accessibility review; decision on virtualisation                                                                                                                             | All §4 targets met in staging                                                           |
| **4. Roll out** | 7–9   | See §8                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | 100% of organizations; old path deprecated                                              |

The API changes are **additive**: the existing "all tasks" query keeps working until no client uses it.

## 8. Rollout strategy

1. **Ship the API first, unused:** the new fields go live behind no flag, because they're additive. A shadow job compares the new summary counts with the old full-load counts for a sample of projects, which catches filter or permission bugs before any user sees them.
2. **Turn the new board on in stages,** per organization, through the `board_v2` flag:

   | Stage       | Organizations                             | Duration    |
   | ----------- | ----------------------------------------- | ----------- |
   | Internal    | Our own                                   | 3 days      |
   | Opt-in beta | Customers with the largest projects (~5%) | 1 week      |
   | Wider       | 25% → 50%                                 | 3 days each |
   | All         | 100%                                      | —           |

3. **Gate every stage** on four checks: p95 board load ≤ 2 s; move error rate < 0.1%; no rise in board-related support tickets; count parity above 99.9%.
4. **Keep a kill switch:** turning the flag off restores the old board instantly. The database changes are expand-only, so a rollback never needs a migration.
5. **Communicate:** release notes from the PM, and a "new board" badge with a temporary "switch back" link during the beta. Support gets a macro for the two visible behaviour changes: counts come from the summary, and cards beyond the first page load on scroll.
6. **Clean up:** two releases after 100%, mark the "all tasks" query `@deprecated`, watch its usage drop to zero, then remove it together with the old board code.

## 9. Risks and open questions

| Risk                                                                                                   | Mitigation                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Counts briefly disagree with the loaded cards after a move                                             | Counts always come from the summary, which is refetched after every move                                            |
| Another user's change isn't visible until a refresh (no real-time updates)                             | Refresh when the window regains focus; `CONFLICT` reloads the affected column. Real-time updates are a separate RFC |
| The summary is the one query whose cost grows with the project (10 → 41 ms from 2,500 to 20,000 tasks) | Cache it per project and filter for a few seconds. Above ~100,000 tasks, maintain per-status counter rows instead   |
| Position keys grow after many drops into the same gap                                                  | Length limit in the database; a periodic rebalance job per column                                                   |
| Old mobile clients depend on the "all tasks" query                                                     | Kept and deprecated, removed only when usage reaches zero                                                           |

**Open questions for product:**

- Is "updates on refresh" acceptable for v2, or is real-time a launch requirement?
- Must column counts be exact at very large sizes, or is "1,000+" acceptable?
- Should each column remember its own sort (priority, due date) or always use manual order?
- What is the mobile app's migration timeline?

# Part 2: Full-Stack Implementation

## Task 2.1: Backend GraphQL API

| Deliverable                       | Where                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| GraphQL schema (type definitions) | [`api/src/graphql/schema.graphql`](../../api/src/graphql/schema.graphql)                                                                                                                                                  |
| Resolver implementation           | [`api/src/graphql/resolvers.ts`](../../api/src/graphql/resolvers.ts), with SQL in [`api/src/repositories/tasks.ts`](../../api/src/repositories/tasks.ts) and batching in [`loaders.ts`](../../api/src/graphql/loaders.ts) |
| Tests                             | [`api/test/graphql.test.ts`](../../api/test/graphql.test.ts) (every result checked against SQL ground truth) and [`graphql-contract.test.ts`](../../api/test/graphql-contract.test.ts)                                    |

Run it with `npm run setup` then `npm run dev`. GraphiQL is at http://localhost:4000/graphql, and http://localhost:4000/dev/users gives a token for every seeded user.

### Design decisions

**The contract comes first.** The SDL is a strict subset of the Part 1 design (a test enforces it), and GraphQL Code Generator types every resolver against it, so drift fails the build.

**Authorization is enforced by Postgres, not by memory.** Each GraphQL operation runs in one transaction as `app_user`, with the caller's id set, so row-level security filters every query. Resolvers get only that transaction; no unscoped database handle exists. Other tenants' ids return `null` or `NOT_FOUND`, never "forbidden", and database messages are masked.

**The query count is constant.** Per-request DataLoaders batch every relation. All board columns page in one `LATERAL` query, and `identifier` and `isOverdue` are computed in SQL. A test proves a board load issues the same number of queries for 5 or 50 cards per column. The summary is one `GROUPING SETS` pass.

**Pagination is keyset-based.** Cursors encode `(sort value, id)`, never timestamps, so JavaScript's millisecond precision can't skip rows. Sorts use index-friendly keys, with undated tasks last. `first` is capped at 100 and query depth at 10.

**`moveTask` is safe under concurrency.** The server computes a fractional rank between the neighbours while holding a per-column advisory lock, so concurrent drops can't produce the same key. A failed mutation rolls back entirely.

**Trade-off:** a transaction holds its connection for the whole operation, so resolvers may only wait on the database. The summary still scans the project on every request, which Part 3 addresses.

## Task 2.2: Frontend Task Board

| Deliverable                         | Where                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| React component (TypeScript, hooks) | [`web/src/features/board/TaskBoard.tsx`](../../web/src/features/board/TaskBoard.tsx) and its children in the same folder                                                                   |
| Tests                               | Unit tests for filters and drag-and-drop maths, a real-cache test of the optimistic move, and component tests for every state ([`web/src/**/*.test.ts(x)`](../../web/src/features/board/)) |

Run `npm run dev`, then open http://localhost:5173. Pick a project and a "view as" user in the header.

| Light, unfiltered                              | Dark, filtered (urgent + high, overdue only)                   |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ![Board in light mode](images/board-light.png) | ![Filtered board in dark mode](images/board-dark-filtered.png) |

### State management and component architecture

**One container, presentational children.** `TaskBoard` owns the filters, two queries (`Board`: columns with their first page; `BoardSummary`: counts and chart data) and the move action. `FilterBar`, `SummaryPanel`, `Board`, `BoardColumn` and `TaskCard` receive props and raise callbacks. Their only state is local UI state, such as an open dropdown, a dragged card or a "load more" spinner.

**Each kind of state has one home, and there's no global store:**

- **Server data** lives in Apollo's normalised cache: each task and column is stored once by id. A column's pages, whether from the board query or that column's "load more" (`taskStatus(id)`), merge into one list.
- **Project and filters** live in the URL, read through `useSyncExternalStore`. Links are shareable, and Back undoes a filter.
- **The session** ("view as") is React context. Switching user resets the Apollo cache, so one user's data never shows for another.

**Moves never refetch the board.** A drop updates the card optimistically and edits only the two affected cached lists. It adds the card only to filtered views that contained it, then refetches just the small summary. If the server refuses, Apollo discards the optimistic layer and the card snaps back.

**Every state is handled:**

- **First load:** a skeleton.
- **Filter changes:** the previous board stays on screen, dimmed.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\mayan\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\bundled-skills\2.1.322\17ea2a244f0fa14ae5a8e9233c3e43ab\dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
  One exception, legend kept: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |
